name: TypeScript in Depth
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Developers who use TypeScript daily and want to master the type system, the JavaScript runtime beneath it and modern tooling for full-stack apps.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of does-it-type-check, predict-the-output, type design and debugging questions.

domains.name: The type system foundations
domains.summary: How TypeScript decides assignability: structural typing, excess property checks, widening and inference, literal types with as const and satisfies, narrowing and type predicates, discriminated unions with exhaustive never checks, and the deliberate soundness holes around any, assertions and arrays.

domains.name: Advanced types
domains.summary: Generics with constraints, defaults and const type parameters, conditional types with infer and distribution, mapped and template literal types, how the built-in utility types are implemented, and variance, overloads and keeping types fast to check.

domains.name: The JavaScript runtime beneath TypeScript
domains.summary: The JavaScript semantics that types do not change: the event loop and microtask ordering, promises, async/await and cancellation, this and closures, coercion and IEEE 754 numbers, and ESM versus CommonJS module behaviour in Node.

domains.name: Designing with types
domains.summary: Using types to model a domain: illegal states made unrepresentable, branded types, errors as values versus exceptions, Zod validation at trust boundaries, end-to-end type-safe APIs, and declaration files and module augmentation for third-party JavaScript.

domains.name: Tooling, configuration and the TypeScript 7 compiler
domains.summary: Configuring and running TypeScript in 2026: the strict family and tsconfig defaults of TS 6/7, module and moduleResolution settings, Node type stripping and erasableSyntaxOnly, the native TS 7 compiler, project references, and publishing libraries with correct exports and types.

domains.name: TypeScript for full-stack apps
domains.summary: TypeScript across a full-stack app: Node fetch, streams, events, workers and graceful shutdown, typed HTTP handlers with request validation, React 19 components, hooks and refs, Vitest typed mocks and type tests, and typescript-eslint rules plus a strictness migration plan.

scenarios.description: Build a fetch-based client whose request and response types come from one source of truth. Validate responses at the boundary, model errors as values, and make impossible request states fail to compile.

scenarios.description: Move a large, loosely typed codebase to strict and the newer checks without stopping feature work. Decide the order of flags, handle the error backlog and use lint rules to keep it from regressing.

scenarios.title: Debugging an async race in Node
scenarios.description: A Node service sometimes returns stale data or crashes on an unhandled rejection. Reason about microtask and timer ordering, cancellation with AbortSignal and promise combinators to find and fix the race.

scenarios.description: Ship a package that works for ESM and CommonJS consumers and for both nodenext and bundler resolution. Get the exports conditions, declaration output and type tests right before the first release.

scenarios.description: Design props, children, events, refs and generic components for a shared React 19 library so consumers get precise inference and helpful errors, and test the types alongside the behaviour.

lessons.title: Structural typing, assignability and widening
lessons.summary: TypeScript compares types by shape. This lesson covers when one type is assignable to another, the extra checks that apply to fresh object literals and weak types, and how literal types widen.

sections.heading: Shapes, not names
Excess property checks on fresh object literals
Weak types
Literal widening
sections.body:
A `const` binding of a primitive keeps its literal type, while `let` widens it, because the value can change:

```ts
let m1 = "GET";   // string
const m2 = "GET"; // "GET"
const req = { method: "GET" }; // { method: string }
```

Object properties widen too, even inside a `const` object, because properties stay mutable. That is why `req.method` is `string`, and why passing it to a parameter of type `"GET" | "POST"` fails. The next lesson shows the fixes (`as const`, annotations and `satisfies`).

sections.heading: Comparing function types

keyPoints: Assignability is structural: required members must be present and compatible; declared names do not matter.
Excess property checks (TS2353) apply only to fresh object literals written where a type is expected.
Weak types (all-optional) reject sources that share no properties with them (TS2559), even from variables.
`let` and object properties widen literals to their base type; `const` primitives keep the literal.
A function with fewer parameters is assignable to a function type with more.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the excess property check protects every assignment.
gotchas.correct: It runs only on fresh literals; a literal stored in a variable first is checked structurally and extra keys pass.

gotchas.trap: Silencing TS2353 with `as Opts`.
gotchas.correct: The error usually flags a typo or a wrong type; fix the key or widen the type deliberately (for example with an index signature).

gotchas.trap: Expecting `const obj = { kind: "a" }` to give `kind: "a"`.
gotchas.correct: Properties widen to `string`; use `as const`, an annotation or `satisfies`.

lessons.lab: In a strict project, declare `type Opts = { retries: number; timeout?: number }`. Assign `{ retries: 1, timout: 5 }` directly, then through a variable, and compare the errors. Make every property optional and repeat with `{ timout: 5 }` to see TS2559.

lessons.title: Inference, literal types, as const and satisfies
lessons.summary: How TypeScript infers types from values and from context, how literal types are kept or lost, and when to reach for as const, satisfies or a const type parameter.

sections.heading: Inference and contextual typing
Literal types and where they get lost
as const
sections.body:
`as const` is a const assertion. It asks for the narrowest type: literal types instead of widened ones, `readonly` properties, and readonly tuples instead of arrays.

```ts
const ROLES = ["admin", "editor"] as const; // readonly ["admin", "editor"]
type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];          // "admin" | "editor"
ROLES.push("x");                              // error: push does not exist on a readonly tuple
const list: string[] = ROLES;                 // error: readonly array to mutable array
```

It is purely a type-level instruction. It does not freeze the object at runtime.

sections.heading: satisfies versus a type annotation
sections.body:
An annotation **replaces** the inferred type with the declared one. `satisfies` (TypeScript 4.9) **checks** the value against a type but keeps the more specific inferred type.

```ts
const a: Record<string, string | number> = { port: 3000 };
a.port; // string | number  (annotation wins)

const b = { port: 3000, host: "x" } satisfies Record<string, string | number>;
b.port; // number           (inferred type kept, value still checked)
```

`satisfies` also performs excess property checks on the literal it checks. Prefer it for configuration objects and lookup tables where you want validation and precise per-key types. Unlike `as`, it never makes an invalid value pass.

sections.heading: const type parameters
sections.body:
Generic inference normally widens: `f(["a", "b"])` infers `string[]`. A `const` modifier on a type parameter (TypeScript 5.0) asks for `as const`-style inference without making every caller write `as const`:

```ts
function routes<const T extends readonly unknown[]>(t: T) { return t; }
const r = routes([1, "a"]); // readonly [1, "a"]
```

Pair the modifier with a `readonly` array constraint, as the release notes recommend.

keyPoints: Contextual typing gives callback parameters their types from where the function is used.
Object properties widen; `as const`, an annotation or `satisfies` keeps literal types where you need them.
`as const` produces readonly literal types and readonly tuples, with no runtime effect.
An annotation replaces the inferred type; `satisfies` checks the value but keeps the inferred type.
`<const T extends readonly unknown[]>` makes inference keep literal tuples for callers.

gotchas.trap: Using `as Config` to "check" a config object.
gotchas.correct: An assertion does not validate the value against the type the way `satisfies` or an annotation does; use `satisfies Config`.

gotchas.trap: Believing `as const` makes an object immutable at runtime.
gotchas.correct: It only changes types; use `Object.freeze` if you need runtime immutability.

gotchas.trap: Annotating a lookup table as `Record<string, V>` and then losing autocompletion of its keys.
gotchas.correct: The annotation replaces the inferred keys; `satisfies Record<string, V>` keeps them.

lessons.lab: Write a `palette` object with one array value and one string value. Annotate it as `Record<string, string | number[]>` and try `palette.green.toUpperCase()`. Switch to `satisfies` and observe that the call compiles while a misspelled value type still errors.

lessons.title: Unions and narrowing
lessons.summary: How control-flow analysis narrows a union: typeof, truthiness, equality, in, instanceof, assignments, user-defined type predicates, inferred predicates and assertion functions.

sections.heading: typeof guards
Truthiness narrowing
sections.body:
`if (x)` removes the falsy values. In JavaScript those are `0`, `NaN`, `""`, `0n`, `null` and `undefined` (plus `false`). That makes truthiness checks risky on numbers and strings: `if (count)` treats a real `0` the same as a missing value. Use `count !== undefined` or `x != null` (which removes both `null` and `undefined`) when zero or the empty string are valid.

`Boolean(x)` and `!!x` test the same truthiness. The handbook notes one typing difference: `!!"world"` is typed as the literal `true`, while `Boolean("hello")` is typed `boolean`.

sections.heading: Equality, in and instanceof
sections.body:
- **Equality.** `===`, `!==`, `==` and `!=` narrow. If `x: string | number` and `y: string | boolean`, then inside `if (x === y)` both are `string`, the only type they share.
- **in.** `"swim" in a` narrows to members that have `swim`. A type where `swim` is **optional** stays in *both* branches.
- **instanceof.** `d instanceof Date` narrows to `Date` and leaves the other members in the else branch.
- **Assignment.** Assigning to a variable narrows it to the assigned value's type, but the assignment is always checked against the **declared** type.

sections.heading: User-defined type predicates
sections.body:
A function whose return type is `v is T` is a type guard: when it returns `true`, callers see `v` as `T`.

```ts
function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  return typeof v === "object"; // compiles, but proves far less than it claims
}
```

The compiler checks only that the body returns a boolean. It does **not** verify that the body actually proves the predicate, so a wrong guard is a soundness hole.

sections.heading: Inferred type predicates
sections.body:
Since TypeScript 5.5, a function with no return annotation can be **inferred** as a type predicate when its body narrows the parameter in both directions:

```ts
const ids = [1, undefined, 2].filter((x) => x !== undefined); // number[]
const t1 = [1, undefined, 0].filter((x) => !!x);               // (number | undefined)[]
const t2 = [1, undefined].filter(Boolean);                     // (number | undefined)[]
```

`!!x` is not inferred as a guard, because a `false` result does not prove `x` is `undefined` (it could be `0`). An explicit `: boolean` return annotation also prevents the inference.

sections.heading: Assertion functions

keyPoints: `typeof x === "object"` does not exclude `null`.
Truthiness narrowing also drops `0`, `""` and `NaN`; prefer `!== undefined` or `!= null` when those are valid values.
`in` narrowing keeps types with an optional property in both branches.
Type predicates (`v is T`) are trusted, not verified.
TypeScript 5.5 infers predicates such as `x => x !== undefined`, but not `x => !!x` or `Boolean`.
Assertion functions narrow by throwing; their call target needs an explicit type (TS2775).

gotchas.trap: `if (count) {...}` on a `number | undefined`.
gotchas.correct: That also skips `0`; compare with `undefined` explicitly.

gotchas.trap: `const assert = (v: unknown): asserts v is string => {...}` and calling it.
gotchas.correct: TS2775; declare it with `function` or give the `const` an explicit function type.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a hand-written `isUser` guard that only checks `typeof v === "object"`.
gotchas.correct: The compiler does not verify predicate bodies; validate every field the type promises, or use a schema validator.

lessons.lab: Write `[1, undefined, 0].filter(...)` four ways (`x => x !== undefined`, `x => !!x`, `Boolean`, `(x): boolean => x !== undefined`) and hover each result. Then turn a guard into an assertion function stored in a `const` and fix the TS2775 error.

lessons.title: Discriminated unions, never and the escape hatches
lessons.summary: Model states with discriminated unions, make the compiler enforce exhaustiveness with never, and know exactly what any, unknown, assertions and the known soundness holes let through.

sections.heading: Discriminated unions
Exhaustiveness checking with never
any, unknown and never
sections.body:
- **any** turns checking off. It is assignable to almost everything (not to `never`), everything is assignable to it, and any property access or call on it compiles.
- **unknown** is the safe top type. Anything can be assigned to it, but you cannot use it (call it, read properties, do arithmetic, assign it to `number`) until you narrow it. Prefer it for untrusted input such as parsed JSON.
- **never** is the bottom type. It is assignable to every type; nothing except `never` is assignable to it, not even `any`. A function that always throws can return `never`.

Under `strict`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` types `catch (e)` as `unknown`, so `e.message` gives **TS18046** "'e' is of type 'unknown'". Narrow with `e instanceof Error`. An annotation on the catch variable may only be `any` or `unknown` (TS1196). `strict` is on by default in TypeScript 6.0 and later.

sections.heading: Type assertions and non-null assertions
sections.body:
`value as T` tells the compiler to treat a value as `T`. It is erased at compile time: there is **no runtime check or conversion**. TypeScript refuses assertions between types that do not sufficiently overlap (**TS2352**, "convert the expression to 'unknown' first"); `as unknown as T` forces it, which is almost always a bug.

```ts
const port = process.env.PORT as number;    // TS2352
const port2 = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000); // real conversion
```

The postfix `!` removes `null` and `undefined` from a type, also with no runtime check.

sections.heading: Soundness holes to know
sections.body:
TypeScript deliberately accepts some programs that can fail at runtime:

- **Array covariance.** A `Dog[]` is assignable to `Animal[]`, so `animals.push(new Cat())` compiles and puts a cat in the dog array.
- **Unchecked indexing.** By default `arr[i]` has the element type even when `i` is out of bounds. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (not part of `strict`) adds `| undefined`, so `const n: number = arr[0]` gives TS2322 "Type 'number | undefined' is not assignable to type 'number'".
- **Trusted predicates and assertions**: `v is T`, `asserts`, `as` and `!` are all taken on faith.
- **Method parameter bivariance**: parameters of methods declared with method shorthand are checked bivariantly even under `strictFunctionTypes` (see the advanced-types domain).
- **any** spreads silently through everything it touches.

keyPoints: Use a required literal discriminant on each union member; optional fields are not discriminants.
`const _x: never = value` in `default` turns a missing case into a compile error.
Prefer `unknown` over `any` for untrusted values; narrow before use.
`as` and `!` have no runtime effect; TS2352 blocks non-overlapping assertions unless forced through `unknown`.
Array covariance, unchecked indexing, unverified predicates and method bivariance are the soundness holes to remember.

gotchas.trap: `default: return 0` in a switch over a union.
gotchas.correct: New members are silently handled; assign the value to `never` (or call `assertNever`) instead.

gotchas.trap: `catch (e: Error)`.
gotchas.correct: TS1196; catch variables can be annotated only `any` or `unknown`. Narrow with `instanceof Error`.

gotchas.trap: `process.env.PORT as unknown as number`.
gotchas.correct: Compiles but the value is still a string at runtime; convert with `Number(...)` and validate.

gotchas.trap: Assuming `strict` turns on `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
gotchas.correct: It does not; enable it separately.

lessons.lab: Model `Loading | Success | Failure` as a discriminated union, render each in a `switch` with a `never` default, then add a `Cancelled` state and let the compiler list every switch to update. Finally enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and fix the new errors.

lessons.title: Generics: constraints, defaults, inference and const type parameters
lessons.summary: How TypeScript infers type arguments from call sites, how constraints and defaults shape that inference, and how const type parameters and NoInfer give you finer control.

sections.heading: Type parameters and inference from arguments
sections.body:
A type parameter is a variable at the type level. At each call TypeScript tries to infer it from the arguments, so you rarely write type arguments by hand.

```ts
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; }
const a = first([1, 2]);        // T = number
const b = first(["x", 1]);      // T = string | number
```

Inference collects candidates from every argument position that uses `T`. If the candidates do not have a single best common type, the call fails rather than silently widening:

```ts
function pair<T>(a: T, b: T) { return [a, b]; }
pair(1, "x");                   // error: "x" is not assignable to number
pair<string | number>(1, "x");  // OK: explicit type argument
```

Type arguments are all or nothing. If a function has two type parameters and neither has a default, `two<string>("a", 1)` is an error. You cannot supply the first and infer the second.

sections.heading: Constraints with extends
Defaults for type parameters
sections.body:
A default (`<T = string>`) makes the parameter optional. The handbook rules are:

- A type parameter with a default is optional.
- Required type parameters must not follow optional ones.
- A default must satisfy the parameter's constraint, if it has one.

A default is a fallback for when nothing can be inferred and no argument is given. When the call site gives inference candidates, inference wins over the default.

sections.heading: const type parameters and NoInfer
sections.body:
A `const` modifier (TS 5.0) asks TypeScript to infer the most specific type, as if the caller had written `as const`:

```ts
function routes<const T extends readonly string[]>(r: T) { return r; }
const r1 = routes(["home", "about"]);   // readonly ["home", "about"]
const list = ["home", "about"];
const r2 = routes(list);                 // string[]: list was already widened
```

The modifier only affects literals written at the call. A variable that was already widened to `string[]` stays `string[]`. Pair `const` with a `readonly` array constraint so the inferred readonly tuple fits it.

`NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4) blocks a position from contributing inference candidates. Use it when one argument should be checked against `T` rather than widen it:

```ts
function light<C extends string>(colors: C[], fallback?: NoInfer<C>) {}
light(["red", "green"], "blue"); // error: "blue" is not "red" | "green"
```

sections.heading: Writing good generic functions
sections.body:
The handbook's guidelines for generic functions are:

- **Push type parameters down.** Use `T` for the element type, not `T extends any[]`, so the return type does not fall back to the constraint.
- **Use fewer type parameters.** Each one should relate two or more values.
- **Type parameters should appear twice.** If `T` appears only once, as in `greet<S extends string>(s: S): void`, it relates nothing. Write `s: string` instead.

keyPoints: Inference collects candidates from every argument that mentions T; incompatible candidates give an error, not a silent union.
Type arguments are all or nothing unless the later parameters have defaults.
A constraint is an upper bound; inside the body T can be any subtype of it.
Defaults apply only when nothing is inferred; required parameters cannot follow defaulted ones.
const type parameters narrow literals written at the call site; NoInfer stops a position from widening T.
A type parameter used only once is a smell: replace it with its constraint.

gotchas.trap: Adding `T = unknown` will make `pair(1, "x")` compile.
gotchas.correct: Defaults are ignored when the arguments provide inference candidates. Pass an explicit type argument or redesign with two type parameters.

gotchas.trap: `const T` makes any array argument a readonly tuple.
gotchas.correct: It only affects array, object and primitive literals written in the call. An already-widened variable keeps its declared type.

gotchas.trap: Returning an object that matches the constraint satisfies a `T` return type.
gotchas.correct: T may be a narrower subtype, so a fresh constraint-shaped value is not a T.

lessons.lab: Write `getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]` and hover the result for two different keys. Then write `light(colors, fallback)` without NoInfer, show that `"blue"` is accepted, add `NoInfer` and confirm the call is rejected. Finally call a `const T extends readonly string[]` function with a literal and with a pre-declared variable and compare the inferred types.

lessons.title: Conditional types, infer and distribution
lessons.summary: Conditional types choose a type by testing assignability, infer extracts parts of a type, and naked type parameters distribute over unions. Knowing when distribution happens explains most surprising results.

sections.heading: The shape of a conditional type
sections.body:
`T extends U ? X : Y` resolves to `X` when `T` is assignable to `U` and to `Y` otherwise. When `T` is still generic the type stays deferred until it is instantiated.

```ts
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type A = IsString<"hi">;  // true
type B = IsString<42>;    // false
```

sections.heading: Extracting types with infer
sections.body:
`infer` declares a type variable inside the `extends` clause. It is bound to whatever TypeScript matches there and can only be used in the true branch.

```ts
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T;
type E1 = ElementOf<number[]>; // number
type E2 = ElementOf<string>;   // string
```

An `infer` can carry its own constraint. The match then fails if the inferred type does not satisfy it:

```ts
type FirstString<T> = T extends [infer S extends string, ...unknown[]] ? S : never;
type F1 = FirstString<["a", 1]>; // "a"
type F2 = FirstString<[1]>;      // never
```

When you infer from a type with several call signatures, such as an overloaded function, inference uses the last signature. That is usually the most permissive one, so `ReturnType<typeof overloaded>` gives the last overload's return type.

sections.heading: Distributive conditional types
sections.body:
When the checked type is a **naked** type parameter and it is instantiated with a union, the conditional is applied to each member separately and the results are unioned:

```ts
type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type D = ToArray<string | number>;       // string[] | number[]

type ToArrayND<T> = [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never;
type N = ToArrayND<string | number>;     // (string | number)[]
```

Wrapping both sides in a one-element tuple turns distribution off. `boolean` is the union `true | false`, so it distributes too: `T extends true ? 1 : 0` with `T = boolean` gives `0 | 1`.

sections.heading: The never edge case
sections.body:
`never` is the empty union. A distributive conditional over an empty union has no members to map, so it returns `never` without evaluating either branch:

```ts
type IsNever<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type X = IsNever<never>;   // never, not true
type IsNever2<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
type Y = IsNever2<never>;  // true
```

Version note: TS 7.1 (beta at the time of writing) adds stricter checks on distributive type parameters in some constraints. Treat that as 7.1 behaviour, not 7.0.

sections.heading: Built-ins that rely on distribution

keyPoints: A conditional type tests assignability and stays deferred while its input is generic.
infer binds a type variable in the extends clause; it is usable only in the true branch and can have its own extends constraint.
Inference from overloaded functions uses the last signature.
A naked type parameter distributes over unions; [T] extends [U] turns that off.
boolean distributes as true | false; never distributes to never.
Exclude and Extract are one-line distributive conditional types.

gotchas.trap: `IsNever<never>` with `T extends never ? true : false` is `true`.
gotchas.correct: It is `never`, because never is an empty union. Use `[T] extends [never]`.

gotchas.trap: `ReturnType` of an overloaded function unions all overload return types.
gotchas.correct: It uses the last overload signature only.

gotchas.trap: Distribution happens whenever a union appears in a conditional.
gotchas.correct: Only when the checked type is a naked type parameter instantiated with a union.

lessons.lab: Define `ToArray` and `ToArrayND` and assign `[1, "a"]` to each instantiated with `string | number`; note which one errors. Write `IsNever` both ways and test it with `never`, `string` and `boolean`. Finally declare a function with two overloads and inspect `ReturnType<typeof fn>`.

lessons.title: Mapped types, key remapping and template literal types
lessons.summary: Mapped types build object types by iterating over keys, as clauses rename or filter keys, and template literal types compute string literal types. TS 7.0 changed how string inference splits characters.

sections.heading: Mapped types and modifiers
Key remapping with as
Template literal types
sections.body:
Template literal types use the same syntax as JavaScript template strings, at the type level. With unions in the slots, the result is every combination:

```ts
type Lang = "en" | "fr"; type Page = "home" | "about";
type Route = `/${Lang}/${Page}`; // 4 members
```

The intrinsic string types `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize` transform literal types. Combined with `infer` they can parse strings:

```ts
type TrimLeft<S> = S extends ` ${infer R}` ? TrimLeft<R> : S;
type T1 = TrimLeft<"  hi">; // "hi"
```

The number of combinations grows multiplicatively, so crossing several large unions can produce very large unions that are slow to check.

sections.heading: TS 7.0: inference by Unicode code point
sections.body:
In TS 7.0, inference against template literal patterns works on whole Unicode code points. Before 7.0 a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as an emoji, was split into two UTF-16 surrogate halves.

```ts
type HeadTail<S> = S extends `${infer H}${infer T}` ? [H, T] : never;
type X = HeadTail<"😀abc">; // TS 7.0: ["😀", "abc"]
```

String utilities that count or split characters this way, such as a `Length<S>` type, can give different results after an upgrade. Tests that pinned the old surrogate-pair results need updating.

keyPoints: Mapped types iterate a key union; -readonly and -? remove modifiers, + or bare adds them.
Homomorphic mapped types over keyof T keep modifiers and map tuples to tuples.
An as clause renames keys; remapping to never filters a key out.
Use string & K before Capitalize because keys can be number or symbol.
Template literal types with union slots produce the cross product.
TS 7.0 infers template literal characters by Unicode code point, not UTF-16 unit.

gotchas.trap: `Capitalize<K>` works on any key from keyof T.
gotchas.correct: keyof T may include number and symbol. Intersect with string first: `Capitalize<string & K>`.

gotchas.trap: Removing a key needs a separate Omit after the mapped type.
gotchas.correct: Remap the key to never in the as clause and it disappears.

gotchas.trap: Template literal inference behaves the same in TS 6 and TS 7.
gotchas.correct: TS 7.0 splits by code point, so emoji-containing strings infer differently.

lessons.lab: Write `Getters<T>` and `Setters<T>` with key remapping, then a `PickByValue<T, V>` that keeps only keys whose value type extends V by remapping the others to never. Build an `EventName<T>` that produces `${K}Changed` keys for an object and use it to type an `on(event, cb)` method.

lessons.title: The built-in utility types and how they work
lessons.summary: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType and Awaited are short mapped and conditional types in lib.es5.d.ts. Reading their definitions explains their edge cases.

sections.heading: Mapped-type utilities
Omit and its loose key constraint
sections.body:
```ts
type Omit<T, K extends keyof any> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;
```

Unlike `Pick`, `Omit` constrains `K` to any property key, not `keyof T`. A typo such as `Omit<Todo, "titel">` compiles and removes nothing, while `Pick<Todo, "titel">` is an error.

`keyof` a union gives only the keys common to every member. So `Omit` on a discriminated union collapses it into one object with only the shared keys. Distribute it instead:

```ts
type DistributiveOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends any ? Omit<T, K> : never;
```

sections.heading: Conditional-type utilities
Awaited
sections.body:
`Awaited<T>` models what `await` does. It unwraps thenables recursively, so `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` is `number`, and it leaves non-thenables unchanged (`Awaited<number>` is `number`).

To get the resolved value of an async function, combine the two: `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>>`.

keyPoints: Partial, Required, Pick and Record are mapped types; Partial is shallow.
Omit<T, K> is Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>> with K extends keyof any, so typos are not caught.
keyof a union is the shared keys only, so Omit on a union loses the variants; distribute it.
ReturnType and Parameters are conditional types with infer; pass typeof fn.
Awaited recursively unwraps thenables; Awaited<ReturnType<typeof f>> gives an async result type.

gotchas.trap: `Omit<User, "pasword">` will flag the typo.
gotchas.correct: Omit accepts any key. Use Pick, or a stricter helper with K extends keyof T, if you want typos caught.

gotchas.trap: `Partial<Config>` makes nested settings optional too.
gotchas.correct: It is one level deep. Nested objects keep their required properties.

gotchas.trap: `ReturnType<typeof asyncFn>` is the resolved value.
gotchas.correct: It is a Promise. Wrap it in Awaited.

Re-implement Omit with `K extends keyof T`, then apply both versions to a discriminated union and to a misspelled key and compare the results.

lessons.title: Variance, overloads vs generics, and fast type checking
lessons.summary: How strictFunctionTypes checks parameters, why method shorthand is still bivariant, when overloads beat unions or generics, and how to keep complex types fast to check.

sections.heading: Parameter variance and the method exemption
Variance annotations
Overloads vs unions vs generics
Keeping types fast to check
sections.body:
The TypeScript performance wiki recommends:

- Extend `interface`s rather than building large intersection types.
- Add type annotations, especially return types, because they can save the compiler a lot of inference work.
- Prefer a base type with subtypes over very large unions.
- Give complex conditional types a named alias instead of writing them inline in a return type, so they are not re-run on every call.
- Build with `strictFunctionTypes` (part of `strict`), which enables faster variance checks.

To investigate, run `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` to see where time goes, and `--generateTrace` to produce a trace you can analyse with `@typescript/analyze-trace`. Deeply recursive types can hit the instantiation depth limit and report TS2589, "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite".

TS 7.0 is much faster, typically 8x to 12x on the projects in its announcement, but the same type-level patterns remain the main cause of slow checking.

keyPoints: strictFunctionTypes checks function-type parameters contravariantly; method shorthand stays bivariant.
Declare callback members with property syntax to get the strict check.
in, out and in out annotate variance; they must match the structural variance and are rarely needed.
Callers see only overload signatures; a union argument needs a union-typed overload or parameter.
Prefer unions over overloads, and generics when output depends on input.
For speed: interfaces over intersections, explicit return types, named conditional types, and measure with --extendedDiagnostics or --generateTrace.

gotchas.trap: strict mode makes all parameter checks contravariant.
gotchas.correct: Methods declared with method shorthand are exempt and remain bivariant.

gotchas.trap: The implementation signature of an overloaded function is also callable.
gotchas.correct: Only the overload signatures are visible from outside.

gotchas.trap: TS 7.0 is fast enough that type-level design no longer matters for check time.
gotchas.correct: Large unions, intersections and deep recursion are still the main costs; measure them.

lessons.lab: Declare an event bus interface twice, once with method shorthand and once with property syntax for `on(handler)`, and assign a handler that needs a subtype to each. Then write an overloaded `parse` and a union version and call both with a union-typed argument. Finally run `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` on a project and record the Check time.

lessons.title: The event loop: tasks, microtasks and await
lessons.summary: How a JavaScript agent runs code to completion, why promise reactions run before the next timer, and how Node adds process.nextTick and phases on top. Includes a verified ordering example that differs between ES modules and CommonJS.

sections.heading: Call stack, job queues and run-to-completion
sections.body:
MDN's execution model describes an **agent** as a heap, a call stack and job queues. A job (a script, a timer callback, an event handler) runs **to completion**: once it starts, nothing else in that agent runs until the call stack is empty.

That one rule explains most surprises:

- A `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback cannot interrupt a running loop. It waits until the current job and every pending microtask have finished.
- A long synchronous computation (a huge `JSON.parse`, a tight loop) blocks timers, I/O callbacks and incoming requests for its whole duration.
- Wrapping synchronous work in an `async` function or a `new Promise(...)` executor does **not** move it off the thread. The executor and the code before the first `await` run synchronously.

To keep a server responsive, move CPU-heavy work to a worker thread or split it into chunks that yield back to the event loop between chunks.

sections.heading: Microtasks drain before the next task
What await actually does
Node: nextTick, phases, and why the module format matters

keyPoints: A job runs to completion; nothing preempts it, not even a 0 ms timer.
The microtask queue (promise reactions, queueMicrotask, await continuations) drains fully before the next task.
Code before the first await runs synchronously in the caller's job.
In Node, nextTick vs promise order differs between CommonJS and ESM entry points; timers come after both.
CPU-bound work blocks the loop; use worker threads or chunking, not async wrappers.

gotchas.trap: setTimeout(fn, 0) runs fn "immediately".
gotchas.correct: It runs on a later task, after the current job and all queued microtasks.

gotchas.trap: Making a function async moves its work to the background.
gotchas.correct: The body runs synchronously until the first await; CPU work still blocks the thread.

gotchas.trap: process.nextTick always runs before promise callbacks.
gotchas.correct: Only from a CommonJS entry point; from ESM top level the promise microtasks drain first.

lessons.lab: Save the A to H program as order.cjs and order.mjs and run both with node. Explain why E moves. Then add a setImmediate inside an fs.readFile callback next to a setTimeout(0) and confirm the immediate runs first.

lessons.title: Promises and async/await in production
lessons.summary: Error propagation through async functions, what happens to rejections nobody handles in Node, picking the right Promise combinator, and cancelling work with AbortController and AbortSignal.timeout.

sections.heading: How errors travel through async code
Unhandled rejections in Node
sections.body:
When a promise rejects and no handler is attached by the time the microtask queue drains, Node emits `'unhandledRejection'` on `process`. The `--unhandled-rejections` CLI option controls what happens next. Its default mode is **`throw`**: if no `unhandledRejection` listener is installed, the rejection is raised as an uncaught exception, and the process exits with code 1.

So one forgotten `.catch` on a background call can crash a whole server. Fixes, in order of preference:

1. Handle the error where the promise is created (`await` it in a `try`, or attach `.catch`).
2. Keep a process-level `unhandledRejection` listener for logging and orderly shutdown, not as normal control flow.

Attaching a handler late (after a timer, say) is still too late: in the default mode the process has already crashed, and with a listener installed or in `warn` mode Node reports the unhandled rejection first and then a `PromiseRejectionHandledWarning` when the handler arrives.

sections.heading: Choosing a combinator
sections.body:
| Combinator | Fulfils when | Rejects when | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Promise.all` | all fulfil (array of values, in input order) | **first** rejection | all-or-nothing work |
| `Promise.allSettled` | all settle (never rejects) | never | partial results; each entry is `{status: 'fulfilled', value}` or `{status: 'rejected', reason}` |
| `Promise.any` | **first** fulfilment | all reject, with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` lists the reasons | first success among redundant sources |
| `Promise.race` | first to settle, fulfil or reject | first to settle rejects | "whichever finishes first", including rejection |

Two points that matter in practice:

- None of these **cancel** the losers. With `Promise.all` the other operations keep running after the first rejection, and with `race` the slow request still finishes in the background.
- `Promise.all([])` fulfils immediately with `[]`. `Promise.any([])` rejects with an `AggregateError`.

sections.heading: Cancellation with AbortController

keyPoints: An async function turns throw into a rejected promise.
try/catch only sees rejections you await inside the try, so use return await inside try.
Node's default --unhandled-rejections mode is throw: an unhandled rejection crashes the process with exit code 1 unless an unhandledRejection listener exists.
all = all-or-nothing, allSettled = partial results, any = first success (AggregateError if none), race = first to settle.
Combinators never cancel the losing operations; AbortSignal does.
AbortSignal.timeout aborts with TimeoutError; a manual abort() gives AbortError.

gotchas.trap: return promise and return await promise are always equivalent.
gotchas.correct: Inside try/catch they differ: only return await lets the catch block see the rejection.

gotchas.trap: Promise.race with a timer cancels a slow fetch.
gotchas.correct: It only stops waiting; pass an AbortSignal so the request is really aborted.

gotchas.trap: Promise.allSettled rejects if any input rejects.
gotchas.correct: It never rejects; inspect each result's status.

lessons.lab: Write fetchJson(url, {signal}) that rejects with TimeoutError after 1 s using AbortSignal.timeout, and a caller that distinguishes timeout from user cancel by err.name. Then run a file that calls an async function which throws without a catch, and note the exit code.

lessons.title: Scope, closures, hoisting and this
lessons.summary: Lexical scope and closures, what each declaration form hoists, the temporal dead zone, and the rules that decide this, including why arrow functions and methods behave differently when passed around as callbacks.

sections.heading: Lexical scope and closures
Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
sections.body:
| Declaration | Hoisted? | Before the declaration line |
|---|---|---|
| `function f() {}` | name **and** body | callable |
| `var x = 1` | name only, initialised to `undefined` | reads `undefined` |
| `let` / `const` / `class` | binding exists but is uninitialised | **ReferenceError** ("Cannot access 'x' before initialization") |
| `var g = function () {}` | only `var g` | `g` is `undefined`, so `g()` is a **TypeError** "g is not a function" |

The period between entering a scope and reaching the `let`/`const` line is the **temporal dead zone** (TDZ). TypeScript catches many TDZ uses at compile time ("used before its declaration"), but not ones hidden behind a function call.

sections.heading: The rules for this
sections.body:
For a normal function, `this` is set by **how it is called**, not where it is defined:

| Call form | `this` |
|---|---|
| `obj.method()` | `obj` |
| `fn()` (plain call) | `undefined` in strict code; the global object in sloppy code |
| `new Fn()` | the new instance |
| `fn.call(x)` / `fn.apply(x)` / `fn.bind(x)` | `x` |

Class bodies and ES modules are always strict. So a **detached method** has `this === undefined`:

```ts
class Counter { count = 0; inc() { this.count++; } }
const c = new Counter();
const { inc } = c;
inc();   // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'count')
```

The same happens with `button.addEventListener('click', this.onClick)`, `emitter.on('data', this.handle)` or `arr.map(this.format)`: the method is passed as a bare function and loses its receiver. (Hosts may pass their own `this`: DOM listeners receive the element, and Node timers pass a `Timeout` object, which can hide the bug instead of throwing.)

sections.heading: Arrow functions vs methods
sections.body:
An **arrow function has no own `this`**. It uses `this` from the enclosing scope, permanently; `call`, `apply` and `bind` cannot change it.

That makes arrows right for callbacks **inside** a method, and wrong **as** an object-literal method:

```js
const o = {
  name: 'o',
  reg() { return [1].map(function () { return this; })[0]; },  // undefined (plain call)
  arr() { return [1].map(() => this.name)[0]; },               // 'o' (inherits from arr)
  bad: () => this,   // the module's this (undefined in ESM), not o
};
```

Fixes for a detached method, each with a trade-off:

- **Arrow class field** (`onClick = () => { ... }`): always bound, but it is created per instance and lives on the instance, not the prototype, so subclasses cannot call it with `super`.
- **`this.onClick = this.onClick.bind(this)`** in the constructor: same per-instance cost, explicit.
- **Wrap at the call site**: `el.addEventListener('click', e => this.onClick(e))`.

TypeScript can help: `noImplicitThis` (part of `strict`) flags functions whose `this` would be implicitly `any`, and you can declare an explicit `this` parameter type.

keyPoints: Closures capture variables, not snapshots of values.
let in a for loop creates a new binding per iteration; var shares one.
function declarations are fully hoisted; let/const/class are in the TDZ until their line runs.
this is decided by the call site; a detached method has this === undefined in strict code (classes, modules).
Arrow functions take this lexically and ignore call/apply/bind.

gotchas.trap: An arrow function makes a good object-literal method.
gotchas.correct: It takes this from the surrounding scope, not the object; use method shorthand.

gotchas.trap: let and const are not hoisted.
gotchas.correct: They are hoisted but uninitialised; touching them early throws a ReferenceError (TDZ).

gotchas.trap: Passing this.handle as a callback keeps the instance.
gotchas.correct: It passes a bare function; bind it, wrap it in an arrow, or use an arrow class field.

lessons.lab: Build a small class with a method and an arrow field, pass both to setTimeout and to [1].forEach, and log this in each. Then rewrite a var-based loop of closures with let and confirm the output changes.

lessons.title: Equality, coercion and numbers
lessons.summary: How == coerces, why === and Object.is differ for NaN and -0, what IEEE 754 doubles can and cannot represent, and when to use BigInt. TypeScript types do not change any of these runtime rules.

sections.heading: === vs == vs Object.is
sections.body:
- **`===` (strict equality)** compares without converting types. Objects compare by **reference**: `{} === {}` is `false`.
- **`==` (loose equality)** converts types first. `null == undefined` is `true`, and both are equal to nothing else. A number compared with a string or boolean converts the other side to a number, and an object is converted to a primitive.
- **`Object.is` (SameValue)** is like `===` except `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true` and `Object.is(0, -0)` is `false`.

Results on Node 24:

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `null == undefined` | true |
| `null == 0` | false |
| `null >= 0` | **true** (relational operators convert null to 0) |
| `"" == 0`, `"0" == false`, `[] == false` | true |
| `NaN === NaN` | false |

The one widely accepted use of `==` is `x == null`, which is true for exactly `null` and `undefined`. TypeScript narrows on it the same way.

sections.heading: NaN and other coercion surprises
sections.body:
- `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself. Test it with **`Number.isNaN(x)`**. The global `isNaN("abc")` coerces first and returns `true`.
- `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is `true` (SameValueZero), but `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is `-1` (strict equality).
- `typeof NaN` is `"number"` and `typeof null` is `"object"`.
- `+` concatenates if either side is a string: `"5" + 2` is `"52"`, but `"5" * "2"` is `10`.
- `Number("")` is `0`, `Number("12px")` is `NaN`, and `parseInt("12px")` is `12`.
- **`Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator compares elements as strings.** `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)` for numbers.

TypeScript blocks some of these at compile time (for example, comparing values with no type overlap), but data that arrives as `any` or from `JSON.parse` still follows the runtime rules.

sections.heading: IEEE 754 doubles
sections.body:
Every JavaScript `number` is a 64-bit IEEE 754 double:

- Decimal fractions are approximated: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, so `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false`. For a tolerance check, compare `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` (scaled to your magnitudes).
- Integers are exact only up to **`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` = 2^53 - 1** (9007199254740991). Past that, neighbouring integers collapse: `2 ** 53 + 1` evaluates to `9007199254740992`. `Number.isSafeInteger` tells you whether you are still in range.
- For money, store **integer minor units** (cents) or use a decimal library. Format with `toFixed` only for display.
- Database IDs and 64-bit counters from other systems can exceed 2^53. `JSON.parse` silently rounds them, so send them as **strings**.

sections.heading: BigInt
sections.body:
`BigInt` represents arbitrary-precision integers: `123n` or `BigInt("9007199254740993")`. `typeof 1n` is `"bigint"`.

| Rule | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Mixing with number | `1n + 1` throws **TypeError** "Cannot mix BigInt and other types" |
| Division | truncates toward zero: `7n / 2n` is `3n` |
| Equality | `1n == 1` is true, `1n === 1` is false (different types) |
| JSON | `JSON.stringify({ a: 1n })` throws **TypeError** "Do not know how to serialize a BigInt" |
| Math | `Math.*` functions do not accept BigInt |

Use BigInt for exact large integers (IDs, nanosecond timestamps, cryptography-style arithmetic), and convert explicitly at boundaries with `BigInt(x)` and `Number(x)`. In TypeScript, `number` and `bigint` are separate types, so the compiler catches most accidental mixing. BigInt literals need a `target` of ES2020 or later.

keyPoints: Use === by default; x == null is the one idiomatic use of ==.
Object.is differs from === only for NaN and +0/-0.
Test NaN with Number.isNaN; includes finds NaN but indexOf does not.
Numbers are IEEE 754 doubles: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3, and integers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1.
BigInt cannot mix with number and is not JSON-serialisable by default.

gotchas.trap: x === NaN detects NaN.
gotchas.correct: It is always false; use Number.isNaN(x).

gotchas.trap: [10, 9, 1].sort() sorts numerically.
gotchas.correct: The default sort compares strings, giving [1, 10, 9]; pass (a, b) => a - b.

gotchas.trap: A 64-bit ID survives JSON.parse as a number.
gotchas.correct: Values above 2^53 - 1 are rounded; transport them as strings and use BigInt if you need arithmetic.

lessons.lab: In a Node REPL, check 0.1 + 0.2, 2 ** 53 + 1, Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53), [NaN].indexOf(NaN), 1n + 1 and JSON.stringify({a: 1n}). Then write a JSON reviver that turns a string field id into a BigInt.

lessons.title: Modules: ESM, CommonJS, top-level await and dynamic import
lessons.summary: How ES modules and CommonJS differ at runtime, how Node decides which format a file uses, live bindings, what top-level await does to the module graph, and when to reach for dynamic import() and require(esm).

sections.heading: ESM vs CommonJS at runtime
sections.body:
| | ES modules | CommonJS |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `import` / `export` | `require()` / `module.exports` |
| Loading | graph is parsed and linked first, then evaluated; imports are **hoisted** | `require` runs the file synchronously at the call |
| Bindings | **live**, read-only views of the exporter's variables | a copy of whatever was on `module.exports` |
| Strict mode | always | only with `"use strict"` |
| Top-level `this` | `undefined` | `module.exports` |
| `__dirname`, `require` | not defined; use `import.meta.dirname` / `import.meta.filename` / `import.meta.url` | available |
| Top-level await | allowed | not allowed |

Live bindings, run on Node 24:

```js
// counter.mjs
export let count = 0; export function inc() { count++; }
// main.mjs
import { count, inc } from './counter.mjs';
inc(); console.log(count);   // 1: the binding is live
count = 5;                   // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
```

With CommonJS, `const { count, inc } = require('./counter.cjs')` copies `count` at destructuring time, so it stays `0`.

sections.heading: How Node picks the format
sections.body:
From Node's packages documentation:

- `.mjs` and `.mts` are always ESM. `.cjs` and `.cts` are always CommonJS.
- `.js` and `.ts` follow the **nearest `package.json` `"type"`** field: `"module"` means ESM, and `"commonjs"` means CommonJS.
- With no `"type"` field, Node uses **syntax detection**: it tries CommonJS and re-runs the file as ESM if it finds ESM-only syntax. Node recommends always setting `"type"` explicitly.

The format matters for more than syntax: it changes `this` at top level, which globals exist, and even event-loop ordering (see the nextTick example in the event-loop lesson).

sections.heading: Top-level await
Dynamic import() and require(esm)
sections.body:
**`import(specifier)`** loads a module at runtime and returns a **promise for its namespace object**. It works in both ES modules and CommonJS, and the specifier can be computed. Use it to:

- lazy-load heavy or optional code (a PDF renderer used by one route),
- load an ES module from CommonJS,
- pick an implementation at runtime.

**`require(esm)`**: current Node lines can `require()` an ES module synchronously (unflagged in v22.12 and v20.19, and no longer experimental in v25.4). It returns the namespace object, with `__esModule: true` added when there is a default export. It only works if the ES module graph has **no top-level await**; otherwise it throws **`ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`**. In that case, use `await import()` or remove the TLA. You can feature-detect support with `process.features.require_module`.

Importing CommonJS from ESM works too: the default import is `module.exports`, and Node detects named exports by static analysis where it can.

keyPoints: ESM imports are hoisted, linked before evaluation, and give live read-only bindings.
.mjs/.mts are ESM and .cjs/.cts are CommonJS; .js/.ts follow package.json "type". Set it explicitly.
ESM has no __dirname or require; use import.meta.dirname, import.meta.filename or import.meta.url.
Top-level await delays every importer until it settles.
import() returns a promise and works from CommonJS; require(esm) fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE if the graph uses TLA.

gotchas.trap: Destructuring require() gives you live values.
gotchas.correct: It copies them once; only ESM named imports are live bindings.

gotchas.trap: A .js file is CommonJS unless it uses import.
gotchas.correct: The nearest package.json "type" decides first; detection only applies when "type" is missing.

gotchas.trap: require() of any ES module works on modern Node.
gotchas.correct: Not if the ES module graph contains top-level await; that throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE.

lessons.lab: Create counter.mjs and counter.cjs as in the lesson and compare live vs copied bindings. Add a top-level await to an .mjs file, require() it from a .cjs file, and observe ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE; then switch to await import().
