lessons.title: Modelling domains with types
lessons.summary: Use discriminated unions so invalid combinations cannot be written, and use branded types so values that share a primitive representation cannot be mixed up.

sections.heading: Make illegal states unrepresentable
Why type aliases do not create new types
sections.body:
TypeScript is **structural**: two types are compatible when their shapes match, whatever their names. `type UserId = string` and `type OrderId = string` are both plain `string`, so this compiles:

~~~ts
function cancel(user: UserId, order: OrderId) { /* ... */ }
cancel(orderId, userId); // no error: both are string
~~~

To get a nominal-like distinction, you have to change the *shape*.

sections.heading: Branded and opaque types
sections.body:
A **brand** intersects the primitive with a phantom property that no ordinary value has:

~~~ts
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" };
type OrderId = string & { readonly __brand: "OrderId" };
~~~

A plain `string` is no longer assignable to `UserId`, and a `UserId` is not assignable to `OrderId`. But a `UserId` is still usable anywhere a `string` is expected. For a key that other modules cannot forge, use a module-private `declare const brand: unique symbol` as the property key. This is often called an *opaque* type.

The brand exists **only at compile time**. At runtime the value is an ordinary string: `__brand` is never set, and `JSON.stringify` writes a plain string. You cannot check for a brand at runtime. Data that comes back from JSON, a database or a cache has to be validated again before it gets the brand.

sections.heading: Smart constructors: one cast, in one place

keyPoints: Replace combinations of booleans and optional fields with a discriminated union, one variant per legal state.
Type aliases are structural; `type A = string` is interchangeable with every other string alias.
A brand such as `string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" }` blocks accidental mixing at zero runtime cost.
Brands are erased at runtime, so values from JSON, a database or a cache must be re-validated before they are branded.
Confine the `as Brand` cast to one validating smart constructor, or use Zod's `.brand()`.

gotchas.trap: Adding `type UserId = string` to stop ID mix-ups.
gotchas.correct: An alias is only a new name for `string`. Use a brand (an intersection with a phantom property) to make the types incompatible.

gotchas.trap: Checking `id.__brand === "UserId"` at runtime.
gotchas.correct: The brand property never exists at runtime. Validate the value's format instead, then brand it.

gotchas.trap: Modelling a request lifecycle as `{ loading: boolean; error?: Error; data?: T }`.
gotchas.correct: Use `{ state: "loading" } | { state: "error"; error: Error } | { state: "ok"; data: T }` so data and error cannot both be present.

lessons.lab: Take a type in your codebase that has two or more boolean flags. List the combinations the domain actually allows, then rewrite it as a discriminated union and fix the compile errors that appear. Next, brand one ID type with a smart constructor and see how many call sites were passing the wrong ID or an unchecked string.

lessons.title: Errors and runtime validation
lessons.summary: Type failures honestly: model expected failures as Result values, narrow unknown catch variables, and parse untrusted input with Zod at every boundary.

sections.heading: Thrown errors are invisible to the type system
sections.body:
A TypeScript function signature records its parameters and its return type. It does **not** record what the function can throw, because TypeScript has no `throws` clause. JavaScript can also throw any value, not only `Error` objects (`throw "oops"` is legal). So the compiler cannot tell what a `catch` will receive.

Under `strict`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` is on, and the catch variable is typed `unknown`:

~~~ts
try { run(); } catch (e) {
  console.log(e.message);            // TS18046: 'e' is of type 'unknown'
  console.log(e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)); // OK
}
~~~

You can annotate the variable only as `any` or `unknown`. `catch (e: Error)` is rejected. The setting does not cover promise callbacks: the `reason` parameter of `.catch()` and the second argument of `.then()` are typed `any` in the standard library typings, so narrow there too.

sections.heading: Errors as values with a Result type
Parse, don't validate: Zod at the boundary
Zod 4 specifics worth knowing
sections.body:
- Zod needs `"strict": true` in tsconfig.
- `z.object` **strips** unknown keys. `z.strictObject` rejects them, and `z.looseObject` passes them through. These replace `.strict()` and `.passthrough()`.
- Top-level formats such as `z.email()` and `z.uuid()` replace `z.string().email()`, which is deprecated.
- Customise messages with the `error` param. `message` is deprecated, and `invalid_type_error` and `required_error` are gone.
- `z.record()` needs both a key schema and a value schema.
- Use `z.enum` instead of the deprecated `z.nativeEnum`, and `.extend` instead of `.merge`.
- Format errors with `z.treeifyError`, `z.flattenError` or `z.prettifyError`. The `.format()` and `.flatten()` methods are deprecated.

keyPoints: Function types do not record what can be thrown; anything, not just Error, can be thrown.
Under strict, catch variables are `unknown` (TS18046 on direct property access); narrow with `instanceof Error`.
Promise `.catch` reasons are typed `any`, so `useUnknownInCatchVariables` does not protect them.
Model expected failures as a discriminated `Result`; let real defects throw to a top-level handler.
Parse boundary data with a Zod schema, use `result.data`, and derive the static type with `z.infer`.
`z.infer` is the output type; `z.input` differs when defaults, coercion or transforms are present.

gotchas.trap: `catch (e: Error) { ... }` to get typed errors.
gotchas.correct: A catch annotation may only be `any` or `unknown`. Keep `unknown` and narrow with `instanceof Error` or a type guard.

gotchas.trap: `const user = (await req.json()) as User;`
gotchas.correct: A cast performs no runtime check. Use `UserSchema.safeParse(...)` and return 400 when it fails.

gotchas.trap: Calling `schema.safeParse(input)` and then using `input`.
gotchas.correct: `safeParse` does not narrow its argument. Use `result.data`, which is typed and has unknown keys removed.

gotchas.trap: Expecting `z.object` to reject extra keys such as `isAdmin`.
gotchas.correct: `z.object` silently strips unknown keys. Use `z.strictObject` to reject them.

lessons.lab: Pick one HTTP handler that casts its request body. Write a Zod schema for the body, replace the cast with `safeParse`, return `z.flattenError(result.error)` with status 400 when it fails, and derive the handler's input type with `z.infer`. Then send an extra field and a malformed email, and check what happens to each.

lessons.title: Type-safe APIs and declaration files
lessons.summary: Share one contract between client and server, remember that types stop at the wire, and type JavaScript you did not write with declaration files and module augmentation.

sections.heading: One contract, inferred on both sides
sections.body:
End-to-end type safety means the client and the server compile against the **same** definition of each request and response. A common setup is a shared workspace package that exports Zod schemas and their `z.infer` types:

- The server parses incoming bodies with the schema.
- The client imports the types with `import type { Order } from "@acme/contracts"`. A type-only import is erased from the output, so no server or database code reaches the client bundle. Under `verbatimModuleSyntax`, importing a type without `type` is error **TS1484**.
- When the contract changes, both sides stop compiling until they are updated.

RPC-style libraries go further: they infer the client's call signatures directly from the server's router type, so there is no generated code. The principle is the same either way: one source of truth, and inference everywhere else.

sections.heading: Types stop at the wire
sections.body:
A shared TypeScript type describes values in **memory**, not the JSON on the wire. `JSON.stringify` turns a `Date` into an ISO string, drops `undefined` properties and functions, and throws on a `BigInt`. If the server type says `createdAt: Date` and the client writes `(await res.json()) as Order`, then `order.createdAt.getTime()` type-checks and crashes at runtime.

Fixes:
- Define the wire shape separately (`createdAt: string`) and convert it explicitly.
- Or parse responses on the client with the shared schema, using for example `z.coerce.date()`, so the client gets real `Date` objects.

The server is also a boundary from the client's point of view. Older deployments, proxies and partial failures all send shapes that the compile-time type never promised.

sections.heading: OpenAPI and other languages
sections.body:
TypeScript types disappear when the code compiles, so a Go or Python consumer cannot use them. When an API is public or polyglot, publish a machine-readable contract. Two directions work:

- **Code-first.** Generate JSON Schema or OpenAPI from the schemas you already validate with. Zod has built-in JSON Schema conversion.
- **Spec-first.** Write the OpenAPI document and generate TypeScript types and clients from it in CI.

Either way, keep **one** source of truth. Do not maintain an OpenAPI file and Zod schemas by hand side by side, because they will drift apart.

sections.heading: Declaration files for JavaScript you did not write
Module augmentation and global augmentation

keyPoints: Share schemas or types from one contract package; import types with `import type` so they are erased.
Compile-time types describe memory, not JSON: Dates become strings, undefined is dropped, BigInt throws.
Parse responses on the client too when correctness matters; the server is a boundary as well.
Generate OpenAPI/JSON Schema from your schemas, or types from your spec, so there is only one source of truth.
Fix TS7016 with @types, then a minimal hand-written `declare module`, and only lastly the any-typed shorthand.
Augmentations patch existing declarations, must live in a module file, and cannot touch default exports.

gotchas.trap: Typing `res.json()` as the server's in-memory type that contains `Date` fields.
gotchas.correct: JSON carries ISO strings. Type the wire format, or parse with a schema that coerces strings to dates.

gotchas.trap: Putting `declare module "lib" { ... }` in a file with no imports or exports to add one field.
gotchas.correct: That declares a new ambient module instead of augmenting the real one. Add a top-level `import` or `export {}`.

gotchas.trap: Submitting types for your own TypeScript library to DefinitelyTyped.
gotchas.correct: Emit `.d.ts` files with `declaration: true` and ship them in the package via `types` or `exports`.

gotchas.trap: Silencing TS7016 with `// @ts-ignore` on the import.
gotchas.correct: Install @types or write a minimal declaration. `@ts-ignore` leaves the module typed as `any` and hides real errors.

lessons.lab: In a small monorepo, create a `contracts` package that exports a Zod schema for an `Order` with a `createdAt` date. Have the server return it and the client fetch it twice: once with `as Order`, and once with the schema using `z.coerce.date()`. Call `getTime()` in both cases and compare. Then augment a library interface from a `.d.ts` file, remove the file's `export {}`, and watch the augmentation break.

lessons.title: tsconfig essentials and the TypeScript 6/7 defaults
lessons.summary: What the strict family really turns on, the two safety flags strict leaves off, how target and lib differ, and which defaults and options changed in TypeScript 6.0 and 7.0.

sections.heading: The strict family
sections.body:
`strict` is an umbrella flag. It turns on `alwaysStrict`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `noImplicitAny`, `noImplicitThis` and `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. Since TypeScript 6.0 (and still in 7.0) **`strict` defaults to `true`**, so a bare `function f(a) {}` now reports an implicit-any error without any config.

You can still opt out of an individual member (for example `"strictPropertyInitialization": false`) while keeping the rest. Future TypeScript versions may add new checks under `strict`, so upgrades can surface new errors even when your config did not change.

sections.heading: Safety flags strict does not include
sections.body:
Two valuable flags sit outside `strict` and are **off by default**:

- **`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`** adds `| undefined` to index-signature and array element reads. `const n: number = arr[0]` then fails with TS2322 ("Type 'number | undefined' is not assignable to type 'number'"), forcing you to handle the empty case.
- **`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`** makes `a?: string` mean "may be missing" rather than "may be `undefined`". Writing `{ a: undefined }` into that type fails with TS2375. If you really want both, write `a?: string | undefined`.

Both flags catch real bugs, but they create churn on large codebases. Turn them on early in a project, or adopt them file area by file area.

sections.heading: target versus lib
sections.body:
- **`target`** controls which *syntax* the compiler downlevels in emitted JavaScript. It also picks a default `lib`.
- **`lib`** controls which built-in *API declarations* (`Promise.try`, `Set` methods, DOM) the checker believes exist.

Neither one polyfills anything. If you set `target: "esnext"` and run on Node 24, APIs such as `Temporal` or `Map.prototype.getOrInsert` type-check but are `undefined` at runtime. Match `target`/`lib` to the oldest runtime you actually support. Add `"DOM"` to `lib` only for code that runs in a browser.

In TypeScript 7.0 the allowed `target` values run from `es2015` through `es2025` plus `esnext`. `es5` has been removed, and `es2026` is a 7.1 addition.

sections.heading: New defaults in 6.0 and 7.0
sections.body:
TypeScript 6.0 changed several defaults, and 7.0 keeps them:

| Option | New default |
|---|---|
| `strict` | `true` |
| `module` | `esnext` |
| `target` | latest stable ES (`es2025`) |
| `types` | `[]`: no `@types/*` packages are loaded automatically |
| `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` | `true` |
| `rootDir` | the tsconfig directory |
| `libReplacement` | `false` |

The `types: []` change is the one teams hit first. Globals like `process` disappear until you add `"types": ["node"]` (or `["*"]` for the old behaviour). With `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` on, `import "./app.css"` needs a declaration such as `declare module "*.css" {}`. In 7.0, `stableTypeOrdering` is always on, so union order in error messages and `.d.ts` output can differ from 5.x.

sections.heading: Options removed in 7.0
sections.body:
Options that 6.0 deprecated are hard errors in 7.0:

- `baseUrl` and `outFile` report TS5102.
- `moduleResolution: "node"` / `"node10"` / `"classic"`, `target: "es5"`, and `module: "amd" | "umd" | "system"` report TS5108.
- `downlevelIteration` reports TS5102.
- `esModuleInterop`, `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` or `alwaysStrict` set to `false` reports TS5108.

`ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"` was only a 6.0 bridge. 7.0 accepts the flag, but the removed options stay removed. The usual `baseUrl` fix is to delete it and write `paths` entries relative to the tsconfig file. The TypeScript team says code that compiles cleanly on 6.0 with no `ignoreDeprecations` should compile identically on 7.0.

keyPoints: strict is on by default since TS 6.0; it bundles nine checks including useUnknownInCatchVariables.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes are not part of strict and default to off.
target downlevels syntax; lib declares APIs; neither adds polyfills.
types now defaults to [], so add "types": ["node"] for Node globals.
baseUrl, outFile, node10/classic resolution and es5 are removed in 7.0; clean 6.0 builds without ignoreDeprecations are the migration path.

gotchas.trap: Assuming strict: true enables noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
gotchas.correct: It does not; enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess (and exactOptionalPropertyTypes) explicitly.

gotchas.trap: Setting target: "esnext" so new APIs type-check on an older runtime.
gotchas.correct: Match target/lib to the runtime; esnext APIs that Node lacks will type-check and then be undefined at runtime.

gotchas.trap: Keeping baseUrl and adding ignoreDeprecations to silence TS 7 errors.
gotchas.correct: Removed options cannot be silenced in 7.0; delete baseUrl and make paths relative to the tsconfig.

lessons.lab: Create a fresh project with an empty tsconfig.json on TypeScript 7. Write a file that reads process.env.HOME, indexes an array and assigns { a: undefined } to { a?: string }. Run tsc and note which lines fail. Add "types": ["node"], then enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes one at a time, and record each new error code.

lessons.title: Module settings and how TypeScript gets run
lessons.summary: Choosing module and moduleResolution, why verbatimModuleSyntax and isolatedModules exist, running TypeScript through tsc, bundlers or Node type stripping, and what the native TypeScript 7 compiler changes.

sections.heading: module and moduleResolution
sections.body:
The modules guide gives a simple rule: **tell TypeScript about the system that will actually resolve your imports.**

- **Code run directly by Node** (compiled by `tsc` or type-stripped): use `"module": "nodenext"`, which implies `"moduleResolution": "nodenext"`. TypeScript then follows Node's rules. The nearest `package.json` `"type"` decides whether a `.ts` file is ESM or CommonJS, `.mts`/`.cts` force the format, `exports` conditions are honoured, and relative ESM imports need a file extension.
- **Code consumed by a bundler** (Vite, esbuild, webpack): use `"moduleResolution": "bundler"`, usually with `"module": "esnext"` or `"preserve"`. Extensionless imports are allowed, and `exports` is read with the `import` condition.

`node10` and `classic` resolution no longer exist in 7.0. `module: node20` models Node's `require(esm)` support. Setting `bundler` for code that Node runs directly hides errors that only appear at runtime, such as missing extensions.

sections.heading: verbatimModuleSyntax and isolatedModules
sections.body:
Single-file transpilers (esbuild, SWC, Node's type stripper) see one file at a time, so they cannot know whether an imported name is a type.

- **`isolatedModules`** reports code that a single-file transpiler cannot handle safely. One example is re-exporting a type without `export type`.
- **`verbatimModuleSyntax`** is stricter and simpler. Any import or export *without* the `type` modifier is kept in the output, and any with it is dropped. Importing a type without `type` reports **TS1484** ("'T' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import...").

This matters at runtime. Under Node type stripping, `import { T } from "./dep.ts"` where `T` is only a type fails with `SyntaxError: The requested module './dep.ts' does not provide an export named 'T'`. `verbatimModuleSyntax` turns that crash into a compile error.

sections.heading: Three ways to run TypeScript
sections.body:
1. **`tsc` emit.** Full type checking plus JavaScript output. Use `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` (TS 5.7+) if your sources import `./x.ts` and should emit `./x.js`.
2. **Bundlers.** They strip types quickly but **do not type-check**. Run `tsc --noEmit` in CI alongside them.
3. **Node type stripping.** Node replaces type annotations with whitespace and runs the file. No source maps are needed. It is stable since v24.12, and Node 26 is the newer LTS.

Node's stripping has limits:

- It rejects syntax that has runtime meaning, with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`: `enum`, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties and import aliases. Decorators and `.tsx` are also unsupported.
- It **ignores tsconfig**, so `paths` aliases do not work. Use `package.json` `"imports"` (`#` specifiers) instead.
- Import specifiers must carry extensions.
- It refuses `.ts` files under `node_modules`.

`--experimental-transform-types` was removed in Node 26, so do not build on it.

Node's recommended tsconfig for this mode is `noEmit`, `target: esnext`, `module: nodenext`, `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, **`erasableSyntaxOnly`** and `verbatimModuleSyntax`. `erasableSyntaxOnly` reports TS1294 for enums, parameter properties and the other non-erasable constructs, so you find them in the editor rather than at startup.

sections.heading: The native TypeScript 7 compiler
sections.body:
TypeScript 7.0 (stable since July 2026) is the native port of the compiler. You install it the usual way with `npm i -D typescript`, and it provides `tsc`.

**Speed.** The 7.0 announcement reports builds typically **8x to 12x faster** than TS 6, with lower memory use. For example, the vscode codebase drops from about 126s to about 11s. Parallelism is part of the design:

- `--checkers` sets how many type-checking workers run. The default is 4, and the flag is experimental.
- `--builders` builds project references in parallel under `--build`.
- `--singleThreaded` turns parallelism off.

`--watch` was rebuilt on a new file watcher, and editors get errors far sooner.

**No programmatic API in 7.0.** Tools that call the compiler API, such as typescript-eslint and the Vue, Svelte, Astro and Angular template tooling, must keep using TS 6. Install `@typescript/typescript6` (binary `tsc6`), often through an npm alias such as `"typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6@^6.0.2"` for those tools. The new API is planned for 7.1, which is in beta. VS Code uses the native-preview extension for 7.0 language service support.

keyPoints: Use nodenext for code Node runs directly and bundler for code a bundler consumes.
nodenext requires extensions on relative ESM imports and respects package.json "type".
verbatimModuleSyntax keeps un-annotated imports and drops import type; TS1484 flags type imports missing type.
Bundlers and Node stripping do not type-check; keep tsc --noEmit in CI.
Node stripping rejects enums, parameter properties, runtime namespaces and import aliases; erasableSyntaxOnly catches them at compile time (TS1294).
TS 7.0 is typically 8x-12x faster but has no programmatic API; API-based tools stay on TS 6 via @typescript/typescript6.

gotchas.trap: Using moduleResolution bundler for a Node server so extensionless imports compile.
gotchas.correct: Use nodenext; the code will fail in Node at runtime if TypeScript does not enforce Node rules.

gotchas.trap: Relying on tsconfig paths when running .ts files with Node type stripping.
gotchas.correct: Node ignores tsconfig; use package.json "imports" with # specifiers.

gotchas.trap: Assuming esbuild or Vite reports type errors.
gotchas.correct: They only strip types; type checking needs tsc (for example tsc --noEmit).

gotchas.trap: Upgrading typescript to 7.0 and expecting typescript-eslint to load it.
gotchas.correct: 7.0 has no programmatic API; give API consumers TS 6 through @typescript/typescript6.

lessons.lab: Create a package with "type": "module" and a src/main.ts that imports ./util and uses an enum and a type-only import without the type keyword. Run it with node src/main.ts and record each failure. Then add erasableSyntaxOnly, verbatimModuleSyntax and module nodenext to tsconfig. Fix every reported error (extension, import type, const object instead of enum) until both tsc --noEmit and node succeed.

lessons.title: Monorepos, build performance and publishing libraries
lessons.summary: Splitting a codebase with project references and tsc --build, making repeated builds fast, and publishing packages whose exports and declaration files resolve correctly for ESM and CommonJS consumers.

sections.heading: Project references
sections.body:
Project references split one large program into smaller projects that build in dependency order. A project that others reference sets `"composite": true`. That setting enforces three things:

- `declaration` is on.
- `rootDir` defaults to the tsconfig directory.
- Every implementation file is matched by `include` or `files`.

The consuming project lists `"references": [{ "path": "../core" }]`. It then type-checks against core's emitted `.d.ts` files instead of re-checking core's source.

Build with **`tsc --build`** (`tsc -b`). It walks the reference graph, rebuilds only projects that are out of date, and supports `--clean`, `--force` and `--verbose`. A root `tsconfig.json` with `"files": []` and references to every package is the usual "solution" config. In TypeScript 7.0, `--builders` builds independent projects in parallel. Plain `paths` aliases between packages give no build boundary: every package's source is re-checked as part of each consumer.

sections.heading: Faster builds
sections.body:
- **`incremental`** (implied by `composite`) writes a `.tsbuildinfo` file. The next build re-checks only what changed. Cache it in CI.
- **`skipLibCheck`** skips checking `.d.ts` files from dependencies, which is often a large share of the time.
- **`isolatedDeclarations`** requires explicit types on exports. Then other tools can generate `.d.ts` files without running the type checker, and builds parallelise better. A missing return annotation reports TS9013.
- **Upgrade to TypeScript 7** for the native compiler's parallel checkers. Measure with your own codebase, because the published 8x to 12x figures are for specific projects.

Type-level performance still matters. Deep conditional types and huge unions cost time in any compiler.

sections.heading: package.json exports and types
Dual ESM/CJS and declaration output
sections.body:
A declaration file has a module format too. TypeScript infers it from the file's extension and the nearest `package.json` `"type"`, just as Node does for JavaScript. In a dual package, pointing both `import` and `require` at one `index.d.ts` makes one of the formats lie about itself, and consumers then see wrong default-import behaviour. Ship **one declaration file per format** (for example `.d.ts` next to the ESM `.js` and `.d.cts` next to the `.cjs`), and nest `"types"` under each condition.

Emit settings:

- `declaration` emits `.d.ts` files.
- `declarationMap` lets "go to definition" jump to your source.
- `emitDeclarationOnly` is for when a bundler produces the JavaScript.

Because Node now supports `require(esm)` for graphs without top-level await, an ESM-only package is a reasonable choice for many libraries. That avoids the dual-package hazard entirely.

keyPoints: composite: true requires declaration and that every source file is matched by include/files.
tsc --build rebuilds only out-of-date referenced projects; --builders parallelises it in TS 7.
incremental writes .tsbuildinfo; cache it in CI for faster repeat builds.
In exports, conditions match in key order: types first, default last.
Dual packages need a separate declaration file per format, nested under import and require.

gotchas.trap: Linking monorepo packages only with tsconfig paths and expecting incremental builds.
gotchas.correct: Use project references with composite and tsc --build so packages build once and consumers read .d.ts.

gotchas.trap: Placing "types" after "default" in an exports condition object.
gotchas.correct: Order matters and the first match wins; put "types" first.

gotchas.trap: Sharing one index.d.ts between the ESM and CJS entry points.
gotchas.correct: Emit a declaration file per format (.d.ts / .d.cts or .d.mts) so each matches its JavaScript.

lessons.lab: Build a two-package monorepo (core and app). Give core composite: true, reference it from app and run tsc -b --verbose twice. Confirm that the second run skips core. Then add an exports map to core with a nested types condition. Emit core's declarations to a separate types/ folder, deliberately move "types" after "default", observe that app loses core's types, and restore the order.

lessons.title: Typed Node.js services: fetch, streams, events, workers and shutdown
lessons.summary: How to use Node's built-in runtime APIs from TypeScript without leaking requests, file handles or in-flight work. Examples target Node 24 LTS (Node 26 is the newer LTS line).

sections.heading: Fetch with cancellation and timeouts
Streams: pipeline, not pipe
Events: typed emitters and the error event
Worker threads for CPU-bound work
Graceful shutdown

keyPoints: fetch resolves on HTTP errors; check `res.ok`.
Cancel requests with `AbortSignal.timeout()` or a controller signal, not a raced timer.
Use `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises` so a failure destroys every stream.
An unhandled `'error'` event throws; always attach an `'error'` listener.
Worker threads help CPU-bound JavaScript, not I/O; messages are structured-cloned.
Shutdown: stop intake, await cleanup in the signal handler, enforce a deadline.

gotchas.trap: Wrapping fetch in try/catch is enough to catch failed upstream calls.
gotchas.correct: A 4xx or 5xx response resolves normally. Check `res.ok` or `res.status` explicitly.

gotchas.trap: `Promise.race([fetch(url), sleep(2000)])` implements a timeout.
gotchas.correct: The race settles but the request keeps running. Pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)` so it is actually aborted.

gotchas.trap: Doing async cleanup in `process.on('exit')`.
gotchas.correct: `'exit'` listeners must be synchronous; pending async work is dropped. Do async cleanup in the `SIGTERM` handler.

gotchas.trap: Making a CPU-heavy function `async` to stop it blocking requests.
gotchas.correct: It still runs on the main thread. Move it to a `Worker`.

lessons.lab: Write a `shutdown.ts` for a small HTTP server: handle `SIGTERM`, call `server.close()`, close a fake DB pool, and force-exit after 5 seconds. Then add a `/slow` route, start a request, send `kill -TERM` and confirm the request still completes.

lessons.title: Typing HTTP handlers, middleware and validation
lessons.summary: Framework-agnostic patterns for typed request handlers: treat input as unknown, validate at the boundary with Zod 4, pass typed context through middleware, and keep response shapes honest.

sections.heading: The boundary is untyped
sections.body:
Whatever a framework's typings say, the bytes in a request body were never checked by the compiler. With the standard `Request`, `await req.json()` is typed `any` when the DOM library is loaded (TypeScript's default `lib`), so this compiles and proves nothing:

```ts
const body: CreateUser = await req.json(); // no runtime check at all
```

Framework generics such as "request body type" parameters are the same thing: an assertion. (Without the DOM lib, `@types/node` types it `Promise<unknown>`, which at least forces a check.) Treat incoming data as `unknown` and validate it. Lint rules such as `no-unsafe-assignment` flag the `any` leaking out of `req.json()`.

sections.heading: Validate with a schema and derive the type
Typed middleware without global augmentation
Typed responses do not strip fields
sections.body:
Structural typing allows a value with extra properties to be passed where a smaller type is expected. Excess-property errors only apply to fresh object literals. So if `row` is a database row with `passwordHash`, then `const dto: UserDto = row` compiles, and `Response.json(dto)` serialises the hash.

Types cannot remove runtime properties. Build the response explicitly (`{ id: row.id, email: row.email }`) or parse it through an output schema with `z.object`, which strips unknown keys. A shared result type such as `type ApiResult<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string }` gives clients a discriminant to narrow on.

keyPoints: `req.json()` gives `any`; annotate nothing until it is validated.
Derive types with `z.infer` from the schema instead of writing a parallel interface.
`safeParse` returns a union on `success`; return 400 with `z.flattenError` details.
Pass auth results through typed context, not an optional global request field.
Assignability does not strip extra properties; build or parse response DTOs.

gotchas.trap: `const body = (await req.json()) as CreateUser` validates the request.
gotchas.correct: `as` is a compile-time assertion only. Use `Schema.safeParse` at runtime.

gotchas.trap: Declaring `interface Request { user?: User }` globally for auth middleware.
gotchas.correct: Every handler then sees an optional user. Pass a typed context from a wrapper such as `withUser`.

gotchas.trap: Annotating a DB row as `UserDto` hides `passwordHash` from clients.
gotchas.correct: The property is still present at runtime and is serialised. Map or parse the object to the DTO shape.

lessons.lab: Write a `POST /users` handler with the standard `Request`/`Response` types and a Zod 4 schema. Send a body with an extra `isAdmin` key and compare `z.object`, `z.strictObject` and `z.looseObject`. Then add a `withUser` wrapper and check that a handler outside it cannot read `ctx.user`.
