questions.scenario: A utils file defines `export const assertDefined = <T,>(v: T): asserts v is NonNullable<T> => { if (v == null) throw new Error("missing"); };` Every call site reports TS2775.
questions.stem: Which change fixes the error?
options: Add `// @ts-ignore` above each call site.
Change the return type to `v is NonNullable<T>`.
Declare it as `export function assertDefined<T>(v: T): asserts v is NonNullable<T> { ... }`.
Return `v` at the end of the arrow function.
questions.explanation: TS2775 says assertions require every name in the call target to be declared with an explicit type annotation. A `const` initialised with an arrow has an inferred type, so the assertion cannot be used through it. A `function` declaration, or a `const` with an explicit function type annotation, satisfies the rule.
rationales: Suppressing the error also loses the narrowing.
That turns it into a type predicate, which needs an `if` at every call and changes the API.
Correct. Function declarations have an explicit type for this purpose.
Returning a value does not give the `const` an explicit type annotation, so TS2775 remains.

questions.scenario: At startup a service loads `const cfg: unknown = JSON.parse(text)`. The team wants one helper call that throws on invalid input and leaves `cfg` typed as `Config` for the rest of the function, with no surrounding `if`.
questions.stem: Which signature fits?
options: `function isConfig(v: unknown): v is Config`
`function validate(v: unknown): Config` implemented as `return v as Config`
`function validate(v: unknown): asserts v is Config`
`function validate(v: unknown): never`
questions.explanation: An assertion function narrows its argument for the rest of the scope once it returns, and signals failure by throwing. A type predicate needs an `if` at the call site, an `as` cast checks nothing, and `never` means the function never returns at all.
rationales: A predicate narrows only inside a conditional.
An assertion inside the helper performs no validation.
Correct. `asserts v is Config` narrows after the call.
A `never` return means the call always throws or loops.

questions.scenario: `interface Shape { kind: "circle" | "square"; radius?: number; side?: number }`. Inside `if (s.kind === "circle")`, `s.radius` is still `number | undefined`, and the code is littered with `s.radius!`.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Keep the interface and enable `strictNullChecks`.
Make `radius` and `side` required with a default of `0`.
Split it into `{ kind: "circle"; radius: number } | { kind: "square"; side: number }`.
Replace `s.radius!` with `s.radius as number`.
questions.explanation: Checking `kind` on a single interface tells the compiler nothing about which optional fields exist. Modelling each case as a union member with a literal `kind` and required fields makes it a discriminated union, so the check narrows to the member where `radius` is a `number`.
rationales: `strictNullChecks` is what makes `undefined` visible; turning it on does not link `kind` to `radius`.
Required fields with fake defaults lose the meaning of the model.
Correct. This is the handbook's discriminated-union refactor.
Another unchecked assertion; same problem.

questions.scenario: `type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle` was just extended with `Triangle`. The team wants every `switch (s.kind)` over `Shape` that forgets the new member to fail the build.
questions.stem: Which patterns achieve this? (Select two.)
options: In `default`, write `const _exhaustive: never = s;`
Give the function an explicit return type such as `number`, return from every `case`, and omit `default`.
Add `default: return 0;` so every path returns.
Add `default: throw new Error("unreachable");`
questions.explanation: Assigning the remaining value to `never` fails with "Type 'Triangle' is not assignable to type 'never'" when a member is unhandled. With an explicit return type and no `default`, a missing case makes the end of the function reachable, giving TS2366. A catch-all return or a bare throw compiles silently and only shows up at runtime.
rationales: Correct. The never assignment is the standard exhaustiveness check.
Correct. TS2366 reports the missing return path under strict null checks.
This silently handles new members and defeats the check.
It fails only at runtime; the compiler is satisfied.

questions.scenario: A shared library wraps `JSON.parse` as `export function parseJson(text: string): ???`. Reviewers want callers to be forced to validate the result before using it.
questions.stem: Which return type should replace `???`?
options: `unknown`
`any`
`never`
questions.explanation: `unknown` accepts any value but forbids property access, calls and assignments to specific types until the value is narrowed, which is exactly the forced validation reviewers want. `any` lets callers use the result unchecked, and `never` would claim the function never returns.
rationales: Correct. Callers must narrow `unknown` before use.
`any` turns off checking for every caller.
`never` means no value is ever produced.
`{}` excludes `null`, which `JSON.parse` can return, and is not the idiomatic safe top type.

questions.scenario: After upgrading to a TypeScript version where `strict` defaults to `true`, `try { ... } catch (e) { log(e.message); }` reports TS18046 "'e' is of type 'unknown'".
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Annotate the clause as `catch (e: Error)`.
Narrow first: `if (e instanceof Error) log(e.message); else log(String(e));`
Set `"strict": false` in tsconfig.json.
Write `log((e as Error).message)`.
questions.explanation: `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, part of `strict`, types catch variables as `unknown` because JavaScript can throw any value. Narrowing with `instanceof Error` handles both real errors and other thrown values. A catch annotation may only be `any` or `unknown` (TS1196), and an `as` cast just assumes the thrown value is an `Error`.
rationales: Not allowed: TS1196, the annotation must be `any` or `unknown`.
Correct. Narrowing is safe for any thrown value.
Turning off `strict` removes many other protections.
Compiles, but crashes or logs `undefined` if a non-Error is thrown.

questions.scenario: `const port: number = process.env.PORT as number;` fails with TS2352. A teammate proposes `process.env.PORT as unknown as number` to make it compile.
questions.stem: What is the correct assessment?
options: Assertions have no runtime effect, so `port` would still hold a string; convert with `Number(process.env.PORT)` and validate it.
Use the angle-bracket form `<number>process.env.PORT`, which performs the conversion.
The double assertion is fine; `as unknown as` converts the string to a number.
TS2352 means `process.env` is typed incorrectly and must be augmented as `number`.
questions.explanation: Type assertions are erased at compile time and never convert values. TS2352 is the compiler pointing out that `string | undefined` and `number` do not overlap; forcing through `unknown` only hides the bug. Real conversion and validation must happen at runtime.
rationales: Correct. Convert at runtime instead of asserting.
The angle-bracket form is the same assertion and gives the same error.
No conversion happens; the value remains a string.
Environment variables really are strings, so typing them as `number` would lie.

questions.scenario: A team lead asks which of these snippets compile cleanly under plain `strict` (no extra flags) and can still fail or misbehave at runtime. `class Dog extends Animal { bark() {} }` and `class Cat extends Animal { meow() {} }` are defined.
questions.stem: Which snippets fit that description? (Select two.)
options: `const dogs: Dog[] = []; const animals: Animal[] = dogs; animals.push(new Cat());`
`const xs: string[] = []; const first: string = xs[0]; first.toUpperCase();`
`const u: unknown = 1; const n: number = u;`
`const p: { x: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 };`
questions.explanation: Arrays are covariant, so a `Dog[]` can be used as an `Animal[]` and a `Cat` pushed into it. Without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `xs[0]` is typed `string` even though it is `undefined` at runtime. Assigning `unknown` to `number` and the fresh-literal excess property are both compile errors.
rationales: Correct. Array covariance is a known soundness hole.
Correct. Unchecked indexing is a known hole unless the flag is on.
Compile error: `unknown` is not assignable to `number`.
Compile error TS2353: excess property on a fresh literal.

questions.scenario: A team with `strict: true` keeps hitting crashes from `rows[i].id` where `i` is out of range, and the compiler never warns.
questions.stem: What change makes the compiler flag these accesses?
options: Nothing; `strict` already includes the check, so the crashes must come from `any` values.
Enable `strictNullChecks` explicitly.
Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, which adds `| undefined` to index access results.
Switch the arrays to tuples; tuples are bounds-checked at runtime.
questions.explanation: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is not part of `strict`. With it on, an index access such as `rows[i]` has type `Row | undefined`, so `const n: number = arr[0]` produces TS2322 and `rows[i].id` requires a check. It is a compile-time change only.
rationales: `strict` does not include `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
`strictNullChecks` is already on under `strict` and does not affect index results.
Correct. The flag models possibly-missing elements.
TypeScript adds no runtime bounds checks, and the arrays are dynamic anyway.

questions.scenario: During a type-design review, four claims are made about `never`.
questions.stem: Which claim is correct?
options: `never` and `void` are interchangeable as function return types.
A value of type `any` can be assigned to a variable of type `never`.
`never` means "possibly undefined" and is narrowed away by `!= null`.
A value of type `never` is assignable to every type, but only `never` is assignable to `never`.
questions.explanation: `never` is the bottom type: it has no values, so it can be assigned anywhere, and nothing else, not even `any`, can be assigned to it. `void` means a function returns no useful value, while `never` means it never returns normally.
rationales: `void` functions return; `never` functions do not.
TypeScript reports "Type 'any' is not assignable to type 'never'".
That describes `T | undefined`, not `never`.
Correct. This is why the exhaustiveness check works.

questions.scenario: Front-end code calls `document.getElementById("app")!.append(view)`.
questions.stem: What does the postfix `!` do?
options: Removes `null` and `undefined` from the type at compile time, with no runtime check.
Throws a descriptive error at runtime if the element is missing.
Acts like `?.` and skips the call when the element is missing.
Converts the element to a boolean.
questions.explanation: The non-null assertion operator tells the compiler a value is not `null` or `undefined`. Like every type assertion it is erased, so if the element is missing the call fails with an ordinary runtime `TypeError`.
rationales: Correct. It is a compile-time-only assertion.
No check is emitted; the generic TypeError comes from calling a method on `null`.
Optional chaining is `?.`, a different operator with runtime behaviour.
That is `!!` in front of an expression, not a postfix `!`.

questions.scenario: A utility in your codebase is declared as `function merge<T>(a: T, b: T): T[]`. A teammate calls `merge(1, "x")` and gets "Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'".
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change if the call is meant to accept a number and a string together?
options: Add a default so the signature becomes `merge<T = unknown>(a: T, b: T)`.
Pass an explicit type argument: `merge<string | number>(1, "x")`.
Cast the second argument: `merge(1, "x" as any)`.
Change the parameters to `a: any, b: any` so inference is skipped.
questions.explanation: Inference takes T from the first candidate (number) and does not widen to a union when the candidates conflict. An explicit type argument tells the checker which T you mean and keeps the call type-safe. Defaults only apply when nothing is inferred, and casts or any discard the checking.
rationales: A default is ignored here because the arguments provide inference candidates.
Correct: an explicit type argument resolves the conflicting candidates while keeping type safety.
Casting to any removes checking from that argument and hides real mistakes.
any parameters turn the function into an unchecked one and lose the T[] relationship.

options: The constraint must be written as an interface, not an inline object type.
`{ length: min }` satisfies the constraint but is not necessarily a `T`, because T may be a narrower subtype such as `string` or `number[]`.
Generic functions cannot read properties of a constrained type parameter.
The return type must be annotated as `{ length: number }` whenever a constraint is present.
questions.explanation: A constraint is only an upper bound on T. The caller may pass an array, and then the function promises an array back, which `{ length: min }` is not. Return `obj`, or change the return type to the constraint if that is what you mean.
rationales: Inline object types are valid constraints.
Correct: the returned object matches the constraint but not every possible T.
The constraint is exactly what allows `obj.length` to be read.
Annotation is not required; returning the constraint type would be a design change, not a rule.

questions.scenario: A router helper is declared `function routes<const T extends readonly string[]>(r: T): T`. Calling `routes(["home", "about"])` infers `readonly ["home", "about"]` as intended. In another file a developer writes `const list = ["home", "about"]; const r = routes(list);` and finds `r` typed as `string[]`.
questions.stem: What explains the difference?
options: Passing a variable disables inference entirely and T falls back to its constraint.
`const` type parameters only work when the constraint is mutable (`string[]`), not `readonly string[]`.
The second file must be compiled with `--target esnext` for const type parameters to apply.
The `const` modifier only affects literals written directly at the call; `list` was already widened to `string[]` at its declaration.
questions.explanation: A const type parameter changes how literal expressions in the call are inferred, as if `as const` were applied to them. An identifier already has its declared type, here `string[]`. Declare `list` with `as const`, or pass the literal, to keep the tuple type.
rationales: Inference still happens; it infers string[] from the variable, and that type also matches the constraint.
A readonly constraint is the recommended pairing; it is not what prevents narrowing here.
Target affects emitted JavaScript and lib, not this inference.
Correct: only literals in the call are inferred in the const style.

sources.title: const type parameters — TypeScript 5.0 release notes

questions.scenario: You maintain `function light<C extends string>(colors: C[], fallback?: C)`. A caller writes `light(["red", "green"], "blue")` and it compiles, because C is inferred as `"red" | "green" | "blue"`.
questions.stem: Which change makes the compiler reject a fallback that is not in `colors`, without the caller writing type arguments?
options: Change the second parameter to `fallback?: NoInfer<C>`.
Change the constraint to `C extends "red" | "green"`.
Give C a default: `<C extends string = never>`.
Mark the first parameter `readonly C[]`.
questions.explanation: `NoInfer<C>` stops the fallback position from contributing inference candidates, so C is inferred from `colors` alone and "blue" is then checked against it. This is the example the TS 5.4 release notes use. Defaults and readonly do not change which positions feed inference.
rationales: Correct: NoInfer blocks inference from that position.
Hard-coding the colors breaks the generic helper for every other caller.
Defaults are ignored when inference finds candidates.
Readonly changes mutability, not which arguments infer C.

sources.title: NoInfer utility type — TypeScript 5.4 release notes

questions.stem: Which statements about type parameter defaults are correct according to the TypeScript handbook? (Select two.)
options: Required type parameters must not follow type parameters that have defaults.
A default overrides whatever type would be inferred from the arguments.
If a type parameter has a constraint, its default must satisfy that constraint.
Defaults are allowed on generic interfaces but not on generic functions.
questions.explanation: The handbook lists these rules: a parameter with a default is optional, required parameters cannot follow optional ones, and a default must satisfy the constraint. Defaults are a fallback when nothing is inferred, and they are allowed on functions, classes, interfaces and aliases.
rationales: Correct: required type parameters cannot follow optional ones.
Inference wins; a default only fills in when nothing is inferred or supplied.
Correct: the default must satisfy the constraint.
Functions can have defaulted type parameters too; the handbook's own example is a function.

questions.scenario: In code review you see `function log<S extends string>(msg: S): void { console.log(msg); }`.
questions.stem: What is the best feedback, following the handbook's guidelines for generic functions?
options: Add a second constraint, `S extends string & {}`, so literal types are preserved.
Keep it: making every string parameter generic improves inference for callers.
Use `S extends any` so the function accepts more types.
Replace the type parameter with `msg: string`, because S appears only once and relates nothing.
questions.explanation: The handbook says type parameters should appear at least twice. A parameter used only once does not relate two values, so it adds complexity with no benefit. A plain `string` parameter is clearer and behaves the same for callers.
rationales: The extra constraint makes it more complex and still relates nothing.
The generic gives callers nothing, because the return type is void.
Widening the constraint changes the contract and still leaves an unnecessary type parameter.
Correct: a single-use type parameter should be replaced with its constraint.

questions.scenario: A helper is defined as `type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;`. A developer writes `const xs: ToArray<string | number> = [1, "a"];` and gets error TS2322.
questions.stem: Which definition makes `ToArray<string | number>` mean `(string | number)[]`?
options: `type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;`
`type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? Array<T> : never;`
`type ToArray<T> = [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never;`
`type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? readonly T[] : never;`
questions.explanation: A conditional whose checked type is a naked type parameter distributes over unions, giving `string[] | number[]`, and a mixed array fits neither member. Wrapping both sides in one-element tuples stops distribution, so T is treated as the whole union. Changing the extends target or the array syntax keeps the type distributive.
rationales: T is still naked, so it still distributes.
Array<T> is the same as T[]; the conditional still distributes.
Correct: [T] extends [any] is not distributive.
Still distributive, and readonly is unrelated to the problem.

questions.stem: Given `type IsNever<T> = T extends never ? true : false;`, a test asserts `const check: IsNever<never> = true;` and fails. What does `IsNever<never>` resolve to, and how do you fix the helper?
options: `never`, because never is an empty union and distribution yields nothing; fix it with `[T] extends [never]`.
`false`, because nothing extends never; fix it by swapping the branches.
`boolean`, because both branches are taken; fix it with `T extends never ? true : never`.
`unknown`, because the conditional is deferred; fix it by adding `T extends unknown` as a constraint.
questions.explanation: never behaves as the empty union in a distributive conditional, so mapping over zero members produces never, and true is not assignable to never. Wrapping both sides in tuples turns distribution off, and `[never] extends [never]` is true.
rationales: Correct: distribution over the empty union returns never; the tuple wrapper fixes it.
never is assignable to everything, including never; the result is not false.
Neither branch is evaluated at all, so the result is not boolean.
With a concrete argument the type is not deferred.

questions.scenario: A library exports two overloads: `function parse(x: string): string;` followed by `function parse(x: number): number;`. You write `type Out = ReturnType<typeof parse>;`.
questions.stem: What is `Out`?
options: `string | number`
`string`
`number`
`unknown`
questions.explanation: When TypeScript infers from a type with several call signatures, it uses the last signature. ReturnType is a conditional type with infer, so it sees only the final overload, which returns number. To get other overloads you need a helper that matches each signature explicitly.
rationales: Overload return types are not unioned by infer.
The first overload is not the one used.
Correct: inference uses the last overload signature.
The match succeeds, so the result is not a fallback type.

questions.stem: Given `type FirstString<T> = T extends [infer S extends string, ...unknown[]] ? S : never;`, what are `FirstString<["a", 1]>` and `FirstString<[1, "a"]>`?
options: `string` and `never`
`"a"` and `never`
questions.explanation: An infer variable can carry its own extends constraint. If the type at that position does not satisfy it, the whole match fails and the false branch is taken. The first tuple starts with "a", which is a string literal; the second starts with 1, so the result is never.
rationales: infer matches only the first element; it does not search the tuple.
The literal type is preserved, so the first result is "a", not string.
The constraint rejects 1, so it is never returned.
Correct: the constrained infer succeeds for "a" and fails for 1.

questions.stem: Given `type Flag<T> = T extends true ? "on" : "off";`, what is `Flag<boolean>`?
options: `never`
`"off"`
`"on" | "off"`
questions.explanation: boolean is the union `true | false`. Because T is a naked type parameter, the conditional distributes: true gives "on" and false gives "off". Write `[T] extends [true]` to test boolean as a whole, which gives "off".
rationales: boolean is not an empty union.
That is what the non-distributive tuple form would give.
Only the true member maps to "on".
Correct: boolean distributes as true | false.

questions.scenario: You write `` type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K>}`]: () => T[K] }; `` and get an error that K does not satisfy the constraint `string`.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Write `Capitalize<string & K>`, because `keyof T` may include number and symbol keys.
Replace `as` with `in` in the key clause.
Add `T extends string` as a constraint on Getters.
Use `Uppercase<K>` instead, which accepts any key type.
questions.explanation: keyof T is `string | number | symbol` in general, and Capitalize only accepts strings. Intersecting with string keeps only the string keys, which is the handbook's own Getters example. Uppercase has the same string constraint.
rationales: Correct: `string & K` narrows the key to string.
The as clause is required for key remapping.
T is the object type; constraining it to string is wrong.
Uppercase has the same string-only constraint.

questions.stem: You need a mapped type that copies every property of T except `kind`, in a single step. Which is correct?
options: `{ [K in keyof T]: K extends "kind" ? never : T[K] }`
`{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } & { kind: never }`
`{ [K in keyof T as Exclude<K, "kind">]: T[K] }`
`{ [K in Exclude<T, "kind">]: T[K] }`
questions.explanation: In a key remapping clause, mapping a key to never removes the property. Exclude returns never for "kind" and the key itself otherwise. Setting the value type to never keeps the key, and Exclude on T itself excludes from the object type, not its keys.
rationales: This keeps the kind key with type never instead of removing it.
This makes everything optional and leaves a kind property.
Correct: remapping a key to never filters it out.
Exclude is applied to T rather than keyof T, so it does not compute the keys.

questions.scenario: A test helper receives a `Readonly<Config>` where some fields are optional, and needs a type with every field writable and required.
questions.stem: Which mapped type does that?
options: `{ +readonly [K in keyof T]+?: T[K] }`
`{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`
`{ readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }`
`{ -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }`
questions.explanation: The minus prefix removes a modifier and the plus prefix (or no prefix) adds it. A plain homomorphic mapped type over keyof T keeps the source's readonly and optional modifiers, so you must remove both explicitly.
rationales: This adds both modifiers, the opposite of the goal.
A homomorphic mapped type preserves the existing modifiers.
This keeps fields readonly.
Correct: -readonly and -? remove both modifiers.

questions.scenario: A team builds `` type Route = `/${Locale}/${Section}/${Action}` ``, where each slot is a union of string literals. After adding more locales, editor responsiveness on files that use Route drops noticeably.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: Template literal types disable type caching for the whole file.
Template literal types are re-evaluated at runtime on every route change.
Template literal types with union slots produce the cross product of all members, so the resulting union grows multiplicatively.
Unions of string literals are limited to 26 members and the extra locales fall back to string.
questions.explanation: Each union in a template literal slot multiplies the number of members: three slots of 10, 20 and 8 members give 1,600 strings. Very large unions are expensive to compare, and the performance wiki advises against them. Types are erased at runtime, so no runtime cost is involved.
rationales: There is no such caching rule.
Types are erased; they never run at runtime.
Correct: the cross product grows multiplicatively and large unions are slow to check.
There is no 26-member limit.

questions.scenario: After upgrading from TypeScript 6 to TypeScript 7.0, a type-level test for a `Length<S>` utility that splits strings with `` S extends `${infer H}${infer T}` `` starts failing for inputs that contain emoji.
questions.stem: What changed?
options: TS 7.0 removed `infer` from template literal patterns.
TS 7.0 infers template literal characters by whole Unicode code point, so an emoji is now one character instead of two surrogate halves.
TS 7.0 limits template literal inference to ASCII and returns `string` for other input.
TS 7.0 evaluates template literal types lazily, so the test needs `--strict`.
questions.explanation: In TS 7.0, inference against template literal patterns works per Unicode code point. Before 7.0 a character outside the BMP was split into two UTF-16 surrogate halves, so a counting utility now reports a smaller length for emoji input. Update the expected values in the tests.
rationales: infer in template literal patterns still works.
Correct: the 7.0 release changed inference to whole code points.
Non-ASCII input is still inferred precisely.
strict is on by default and unrelated to this change.

questions.stem: Consider `type Strs<T> = { [K in keyof T]: string };`, a homomorphic mapped type. Which statements are true? (Select two.)
options: `Strs<{ readonly a?: number }>` keeps `a` as readonly and optional.
`Strs<[1, 2]>` is `[string, string]`, a tuple, not an object with numeric keys.
Homomorphic mapped types always drop the source's optional modifiers.
`Strs<T>` evaluates to `{}` for any tuple type T.
questions.explanation: A mapped type over keyof T for a type parameter T is homomorphic: it keeps the readonly and optional modifiers of the source properties. When T is instantiated with an array or tuple type, the result is an array or tuple of the mapped element types.
rationales: Correct: homomorphic mapped types preserve modifiers.
Correct: mapping over a tuple gives a tuple.
Modifiers are kept unless you remove them with -?.
Tuples map element by element; they do not become {}.

sources.title: Mapped types on tuples and arrays — TypeScript 3.1 release notes

questions.scenario: A reviewer notices `type PublicUser = Omit<User, "pasword">;` (misspelled). The code compiles and `PublicUser` still has a `password` field.
questions.stem: Why did the compiler not flag the typo?
options: Omit only checks keys under `--strict`, which is off in this project.
Omit silently converts unknown keys to an index signature.
Omit is defined as `Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>` with `K extends keyof any`, so any property key is accepted.
String literal arguments to utility types are widened to `string`.
questions.explanation: Unlike Pick, whose K is constrained to keyof T, Omit constrains K to any property key. Excluding a key that does not exist removes nothing. A stricter helper with `K extends keyof T` catches typos.
rationales: Omit's constraint does not depend on strict, and strict is on by default in TS 6 and 7.
No index signature is added.
Correct: the loose `keyof any` constraint accepts any key.
Literal type arguments are not widened.

questions.scenario: You have `type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number; id: string } | { kind: "square"; side: number; id: string }` and define `type NewShape = Omit<Shape, "id">`. Now `{ kind: "circle", r: 1 }` fails to type-check as a NewShape.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Use `Partial<Omit<Shape, "id">>`.
Use `Omit<Shape, "id" | "r" | "side">`.
Use a distributive helper: `type DOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends any ? Omit<T, K> : never;`.
Use `Exclude<Shape, { id: string }>`.
questions.explanation: keyof a union gives only the keys common to all members (`kind | id`), so Omit collapses the union to `{ kind: "circle" | "square" }`. A distributive conditional applies Omit to each member separately and keeps the discriminated union. Partial or Exclude does not restore the variant-specific properties.
rationales: Partial hides the problem by making everything optional and still loses r and side.
This removes even more properties.
Correct: distributing Omit over the union keeps each variant.
Every member has an id, so Exclude removes them all and gives never.

questions.scenario: `updateSettings(patch: Partial<Settings>)` is called with `{ theme: { mode: "dark" } }`, where `Settings.theme` is `{ mode: string; accent: string }`. The call fails because `accent` is missing.
questions.stem: What explains this?
options: Partial requires `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` to apply to nested objects.
Partial only works on interfaces, not on type aliases.
Object literals passed to Partial are checked for excess properties, and mode is treated as excess.
Partial is shallow: it makes `theme` optional but leaves the properties inside `theme` required.
questions.explanation: Partial is defined as `{ [P in keyof T]?: T[P] }`, so only the top-level properties become optional and T[P] is unchanged. Nested updates need a recursive DeepPartial type, or a separate patch type for the nested object.
rationales: That flag concerns undefined in optional properties, not depth.
Partial works on any object type.
mode is a known property, so it is not excess.
Correct: Partial maps one level only.

questions.stem: Given `async function loadUser(id: string) { return { id, name: "Ada" }; }`, which type gives the user object without the Promise?
options: `ReturnType<loadUser>`
`ReturnType<typeof loadUser>`
`Awaited<typeof loadUser>`
`Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>>`
questions.explanation: ReturnType takes a function type, so you pass `typeof loadUser`, and for an async function it gives a Promise. Awaited unwraps the Promise recursively to the resolved value type.
rationales: loadUser is a value, so you need typeof to use it as a type.
This gives `Promise<{ id: string; name: string }>`.
Awaited of a function type leaves it unchanged, because it is not thenable.
Correct: ReturnType gives the Promise and Awaited unwraps it.

questions.scenario: A feature-flag map is typed `const flags: Record<"search" | "export" | "beta", boolean> = { search: true, export: false };`. The compiler reports that `beta` is missing. Only some flags are configured in each environment.
questions.stem: Which type models that intent?
options: `Record<string, boolean>`
`Record<"search" | "export" | "beta", boolean | undefined>`
`Partial<Record<"search" | "export" | "beta", boolean>>`
`Pick<Record<"search" | "export" | "beta", boolean>, "search">`
questions.explanation: Record maps every member of the key union to a required property. Wrapping it in Partial makes each key optional and still rejects unknown flag names. `Record<string, boolean>` loses the key checking, and `boolean | undefined` still requires every key to be present.
rationales: This allows any misspelled flag name.
The keys are still required, though the values may be undefined.
Correct: the keys are known but each one is optional.
This allows only the search flag.

questions.stem: Which of these match how the TypeScript standard library defines these utility types? (Select two.)
options: `type Partial<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] };`
`type Omit<T, K extends keyof T> = Pick<T, Extract<keyof T, K>>;`
`type ReturnType<T extends (...args: any) => any> = T extends (...args: any) => infer R ? R : any;`
`type Required<T> = { +readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P] };`
questions.explanation: Partial is a mapped type that adds the optional modifier, and ReturnType is a conditional type that infers the return type. The library defines Omit with Exclude and `K extends keyof any`, and Required removes the optional modifier with -? rather than adding readonly.
rationales: Correct: this is the lib.es5.d.ts definition.
Extract would keep the named keys, and the real constraint is keyof any.
Correct: this is the lib definition.
Required uses `-?`; adding readonly is what Readonly does.

questions.scenario: With `strict` on, an event bus contract is declared with method shorthand: `type Bus = { dispatch(e: BaseEvent): void }`. A plugin assigns `{ dispatch(e: ClickEvent) { e.x.toFixed(); } }` and it compiles, then crashes at runtime on a non-click event.
questions.stem: How should `dispatch` be declared so the compiler rejects this assignment?
options: Keep the method syntax and add `strictFunctionTypes: true` explicitly in tsconfig.
Mark the interface `readonly`.
Change the parameter to `e: unknown` in the plugin.
Use property syntax: `type Bus = { dispatch: (e: BaseEvent) => void }`.
questions.explanation: strictFunctionTypes checks parameters of function types contravariantly, but parameters of methods declared with method shorthand are exempt and stay bivariant. Declaring dispatch as a function-typed property makes the assignment of a ClickEvent-only handler an error. strict already enables strictFunctionTypes, so setting it again changes nothing.
rationales: strictFunctionTypes is already on under strict, and methods are exempt from it.
readonly affects writes to properties, not parameter variance.
That changes the plugin, not the contract, and does not prevent the next unsafe plugin.
Correct: function-typed properties get contravariant parameter checks.

questions.scenario: A function is declared with two overloads, `len(s: string): number` and `len(a: unknown[]): number`, and a shared implementation. A caller has `const v: string | unknown[]` and `len(v)` fails with "No overload matches this call".
questions.stem: What is the best change to the library?
options: Add the implementation signature `len(x: any)` to the public overload list as-is, so callers get an unchecked catch-all.
Ask callers to cast: `len(v as string)`.
Replace the overloads with a single signature `len(x: string | unknown[]): number`.
Make it generic: `len<T>(x: T): number`.
questions.explanation: Each call must match a single overload, and neither accepts the union. The handbook advises preferring union-typed parameters over overloads when the return type is the same. An `any` catch-all or casts give up type checking, and an unconstrained generic accepts anything.
rationales: An any overload accepts anything and hides mistakes.
Casting lies to the compiler and pushes the problem to every caller.
Correct: a union parameter is simpler and accepts the union argument.
An unconstrained T accepts numbers and objects, and T is used only once.

options: Overloaded functions must have at least two overload signatures.
Only the overload signatures are visible to callers; the implementation signature cannot be called directly.
The implementation must return the union of the overload return types.
Overloads require explicit return annotations on the implementation.
questions.explanation: The handbook states that the implementation signature is not visible from outside. Callers see only `fmt(x: string)`, so a number argument is rejected. Add an overload for number if callers need it.
rationales: A single overload plus an implementation is valid.
Correct: the implementation signature is hidden from callers.
The return type of the implementation is not the issue.
Return annotations are optional here.

questions.scenario: Type checking in a large monorepo has become slow. Several core types are built as intersections of many object aliases (`type Model = A & B & C & D & ...`), and many exported functions rely on deep inferred return types.
questions.stem: Which actions follow the TypeScript performance wiki's guidance? (Select two.)
options: Run `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` (and `--generateTrace` if needed) to find where check time goes.
Convert interfaces that use `extends` into intersection type aliases so they are cached.
Replace the large intersections with interfaces that `extend` the parts.
Turn off `strict`, since strictness checks dominate check time.
questions.explanation: The wiki recommends extending interfaces rather than building large intersection types, and adding explicit return type annotations. It also documents --extendedDiagnostics and --generateTrace for investigating slow builds. Converting interfaces into intersections is the opposite of the advice, and disabling strict loses safety; the wiki even recommends strictFunctionTypes for faster variance checks.
rationales: Correct: measuring first is the documented approach.
This is the reverse of the advice: interfaces over intersections.
Correct: interface extension is easier to check than large intersections.
This trades safety for no targeted gain; the wiki actually recommends building with strictFunctionTypes (part of strict) because it enables faster variance checks.

questions.scenario: A colleague proposes adding variance annotations everywhere, for example `interface Store<out T> { get: () => T; set: (v: T) => void }`, "to make checks faster".
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Agree: annotations are required for generic interfaces under strict.

Disagree: `out` here contradicts the structure, because T is also used in a parameter position. TypeScript infers variance automatically and annotations should only be written when they match the structural variance.
Agree, but use `in` instead, because setters are more common than getters.
Disagree: variance annotations are only allowed on classes.
questions.explanation: T appears in both a return position and a parameter position, so Store is structurally invariant (`in out`). The handbook warns never to write an annotation that does not match the structural variance and notes that annotations are almost never necessary (at most a small benefit in extraordinarily complex types, after profiling), because variance is measured automatically. Here the compiler rejects the annotation with an error that the type is not assignable "as implied by variance annotation".
rationales: Annotations are optional; variance is inferred.
Correct: the annotation contradicts how T is used, and it is unnecessary.
`in` is equally wrong for a type used in both positions.
They are allowed on interfaces and type aliases too, as the handbook examples show.

questions.scenario: A design system models every HTML element with a union of several hundred object types (`type Element = DivEl | SpanEl | ...`). Functions accepting `Element` are slow to check, and assignment errors are hard to read.
questions.stem: Which change does the TypeScript performance wiki suggest?
options: Split the union into two smaller unions and intersect them.
Replace the union with a template literal type that produces the element names.
Wrap the union in `NoInfer<Element>` wherever it is used as a parameter.
Introduce a base type such as `HtmlElement` that the variants extend, and accept the base type where the specific variant does not matter.
questions.explanation: Checking assignability against a very large union means comparing against many members. The performance wiki suggests modelling shared structure with a base type and subtypes instead of a huge union, using its own HtmlElement example. Intersections and template literal unions add work, and NoInfer only affects inference.
rationales: Intersecting unions makes the checker do more work, not less.
Template literal unions can be large too, and they describe strings, not element objects.
NoInfer only affects inference and does nothing for assignability cost.
Correct: a base type with subtypes is cheaper than a huge union.

questions.stem: Run with Node 24, what does it print?
options: A F H C D G B E
A F H E C D G B
A H F E C D G B
A F H C D G E B
questions.explanation: Synchronous code prints A, F (the async function runs synchronously until its first await) and H. In an ES module, top-level code already runs inside a promise job, so the promise microtasks C, D and G drain before the nextTick queue (E). The timer B always comes last.
rationales: Timers are tasks and run after both the nextTick and microtask queues, so B cannot come before E.
This is the order for the same code as CommonJS (.cts/.cjs), where nextTick runs before promise microtasks.
F is logged synchronously when the async IIFE is called, before H.
Correct. This is the ES module order observed on Node 24.

questions.scenario: A developer copies a working ordering test from `order.mts` into `order.cts` without changing a line. The relative order of a `process.nextTick` callback and a `Promise.resolve().then` callback flips.
questions.stem: What explains the difference?
options: process.nextTick is unavailable in ES modules, so Node polyfills it with a timer.
.cts files are compiled by tsc to use setImmediate instead of promises.
In CommonJS, the nextTick queue is processed after the main script before promise microtasks; ESM top-level code runs inside a promise job, so microtasks drain first.
Promises are slower in CommonJS because CommonJS modules are not strict.
questions.explanation: Node processes the nextTick queue and the promise microtask queue between operations. A CommonJS main script finishes as a plain job, and Node then runs nextTick callbacks first. An ES module is evaluated from within a promise job, so the microtask queue drains before control returns to Node's nextTick processing.
rationales: process.nextTick works in ES modules; the order just differs.
Type stripping or compilation does not rewrite promise callbacks into setImmediate.
Correct. The module format changes which queue is processed first.
Strict mode has no effect on scheduling.

sources.title: Event loop, timers and nextTick — Node.js Learn

options: sync t1 p1 q p2
sync p1 p2 q t1
sync p1 q p2 t1
sync p1 q t1 p2
questions.explanation: After the synchronous log, the microtask queue holds p1 and q in that order. Running p1 queues p2 at the back of the microtask queue, after q. The queue is drained completely, including newly added microtasks, before the timer task t1 runs.
rationales: A 0 ms timer is a task and cannot run before pending microtasks.
p2 is queued while p1 runs, so it goes behind q, which was already waiting.
Correct. Microtasks run in FIFO order and the queue drains fully before the timer.
Microtasks added during the drain still run before the next task, so p2 comes before t1.

questions.scenario: An API handler synchronously parses a 200 MB JSON upload, which takes about two seconds. During that time the health-check endpoint times out and a `setInterval` heartbeat stops firing. A teammate proposes several fixes.
questions.stem: Which fix actually keeps the server responsive?
options: Move the parsing to a worker thread, or process the data in chunks that yield to the event loop between chunks.
Mark the handler async and await the JSON.parse call.
Wrap JSON.parse in new Promise((resolve) => resolve(JSON.parse(body))).
Lower the heartbeat interval to 0 ms so it gets higher priority.
questions.explanation: A job runs to completion, so a two-second synchronous parse blocks every other callback on that thread. Making the work async or putting it in a promise executor does not move it off the thread. The executor and the code before the first await run synchronously. Only moving the work to another thread, or breaking it into pieces that give the loop a turn, lets timers and requests run.
rationales: Correct. The work leaves the main thread or yields between chunks.
await on a non-promise value does not make JSON.parse itself asynchronous; the parse still blocks.
A promise executor runs synchronously, so the parse still blocks the thread.
Timers have no priority over a running job; a 0 ms interval still waits for the parse to finish.

sources.title: Event loop, timers and nextTick — Node.js Learn

questions.stem: Which statements about the microtask queue are correct? (Select two.)
options: It is drained completely, including microtasks queued during the drain, before the next task runs.
A callback that keeps queueing new microtasks can prevent timers and I/O from ever running.
A setTimeout(fn, 0) scheduled earlier runs before promise reactions queued later in the same job.
await always waits for at least one timer task before continuing.
questions.explanation: Microtasks run after the current job and the queue is emptied fully before the event loop picks another task. That is why an endless microtask chain starves timers and I/O. Timers are tasks, so they wait for all pending microtasks. An await continuation is a microtask, not a timer task.
rationales: Correct. The queue is drained to empty before the next task.
Correct. Endless microtasks starve the event loop.
Timers are tasks and run after all pending microtasks, whichever was scheduled first.
The continuation after await is a microtask; it runs before already-queued timers.

questions.stem: What is the minimal correct fix?
options: Change the line to return await db.findUser(id);
Remove async from the function so the try/catch becomes synchronous.
Add .catch(() => {}) after db.findUser(id) so the error is swallowed.
Wrap the call in Promise.resolve(db.findUser(id)).
questions.explanation: Returning the promise without awaiting it leaves the try block at once; the rejection is never thrown inside the try, so the catch never runs. With return await, the rejection is thrown inside the try block and the catch handles it. Swallowing the error with an empty catch returns undefined instead of the cached value.
rationales: Correct. Awaiting inside the try makes the rejection catchable there.
A synchronous try cannot catch a later promise rejection either.
This hides the failure and resolves to undefined instead of falling back to the cache.
Promise.resolve of a promise returns the same rejecting promise; nothing is caught.

questions.scenario: A dashboard loads five independent widgets in parallel. Today it uses `Promise.all`, and when any one widget's API fails, the whole dashboard shows an error page even though the other four responses arrived.
questions.stem: Which change best fits the requirement to show every widget that loaded and an error tile for those that failed?
options: Keep Promise.all but call the five APIs one after another.
Use Promise.race so the first widget to load is shown.
Use Promise.any so the dashboard renders once any widget succeeds.
Use Promise.allSettled and render each result based on its status.
questions.explanation: Promise.allSettled waits for every input and never rejects. Each result is an object with status fulfilled and a value, or status rejected and a reason. That maps directly onto showing widgets plus error tiles. Promise.all rejects on the first failure and discards the other results.
rationales: Running them sequentially is slower and still fails as a whole on the first rejection.
race settles with only the first result to arrive, so the rest are lost.
any gives only the first success and ignores the others.
Correct. allSettled gives per-input outcomes for partial rendering.

questions.scenario: A client can fetch the same static manifest from three mirror CDNs. It should use whichever mirror answers successfully first, and report an error only if all three fail.
questions.stem: Which combinator matches this behaviour?
options: Promise.any
Promise.race
Promise.all
Promise.allSettled
questions.explanation: Promise.any fulfils with the first input that fulfils and ignores rejections unless every input rejects, in which case it rejects with an AggregateError listing all the reasons. Promise.race would settle with the first mirror to fail if that failure arrived first.
rationales: Correct. First success wins, and it fails only when all inputs reject.
race settles on the first result, including a fast rejection, which would fail the load even if another mirror is healthy.
all needs every mirror to succeed and returns all three manifests.
allSettled waits for all three and never rejects, so you would have to choose the result yourself and wait for the slowest mirror.

questions.scenario:
A service enforces a two-second budget on calls to a partner API:

```ts
const res = await Promise.race([
  fetch(url),
  new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("timeout")), 2000)),
]);
```

Under load, the process runs out of sockets even though callers see timeouts on time.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Increase the timeout so fewer requests are abandoned.
Pass { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) } to fetch so the request itself is aborted.
Replace Promise.race with Promise.any.
Wrap the race in a second Promise.race with a longer timer.
questions.explanation: Promise.race stops waiting for the fetch but does not cancel it, so abandoned requests keep their sockets until the partner answers. Passing an AbortSignal makes fetch abort the underlying request. AbortSignal.timeout creates a signal that aborts itself after the given time with a TimeoutError.
rationales: A longer timeout still leaves abandoned requests running; it just changes when.
Correct. A signal really cancels the request and frees its resources.
any ignores the timer rejection and still does not cancel the fetch.
Nesting races changes nothing about cancellation.

questions.stem: Which rewrites wait for every save and surface failures to the caller? (Select two.)
options: for (const r of records) { await save(r); }
await Promise.all(records.map((r) => save(r)));
await records.forEach(async (r) => { await save(r); });
records.forEach((r) => { void save(r); });
questions.explanation: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so nothing waits and rejections have no handler. A for...of loop with await runs the saves one at a time. Promise.all over a mapped array runs them concurrently. Both reject to the caller on failure.
rationales: Correct. This is sequential and awaits each save.
Correct. This is concurrent, and the first failure rejects the awaited promise.
forEach returns undefined, so awaiting it waits for nothing.
void explicitly discards the promise; nothing waits and failures go unhandled.

questions.scenario: A Node 24 service calls `sendMetrics()`, an async function, without `await` or `.catch`. The metrics endpoint goes down and the service starts restarting repeatedly. There is no `unhandledRejection` listener.
questions.stem: Why does the process exit?
options: Node exits on any rejection, handled or not, unless --unhandled-rejections=warn is set.
Async functions that are not awaited run on a separate thread that kills the process on error.
Node's default unhandled-rejection mode is throw, so the unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception and the process exits.
TypeScript inserts a process.exit call for floating promises when compiling.
questions.explanation: In the default throw mode, Node emits unhandledRejection, and if no listener handles it, raises the rejection as an uncaught exception, which ends the process with exit code 1. The fix is to handle the error where the promise is created, for example by attaching .catch with logging. A process-level listener is a safety net, not the fix.
rationales: Handled rejections are normal control flow and do not end the process.
Async functions run on the same thread; there is no separate thread.
Correct. This is the documented default behaviour of --unhandled-rejections.
TypeScript emits no such code; floating promises type-check silently.

questions.scenario: A search box cancels the previous request whenever the user types (`controller.abort()`), and every request also has `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)` combined into its signal. The UI must show "Request timed out" only for real timeouts and stay silent on user cancellation.
questions.stem: How should the catch block tell the two cases apart?
options: Check err.message for the substring "3000".
Treat every DOMException as a timeout.
Check err.name: "TimeoutError" for the timeout signal and "AbortError" for the manual abort.
Compare the elapsed time with 3000 ms using Date.now().
questions.explanation: MDN documents that AbortSignal.timeout aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException, while AbortController.abort() with no reason gives an AbortError. fetch rejects with the signal's reason, so err.name distinguishes the two cases reliably. Message text and timing heuristics are fragile.
rationales: Error messages are not specified for this purpose and do not include the timeout value.
Both cases produce DOMExceptions, so this would show timeouts on every keystroke.
Correct. The error names differ by design.
Timing is approximate and a cancel near 3 s would be misclassified.

questions.stem: Which change makes onDone always update the instance? Choose the most direct fix.
options: Change private count to public count.
Declare onDone as a static method.
Register it as emitter.on("done", () => this.onDone()).
Mark onDone as async.
questions.explanation: Passing this.onDone hands over a bare function, so its this is decided by whoever calls it, not by the class. Wrapping it in an arrow function at the call site captures the instance lexically and calls onDone as a method. A bound method or an arrow class field would also work.
rationales: Visibility modifiers are type-only and do not affect this at runtime.
A static method has no instance state at all.
Correct. The arrow keeps the instance as the receiver.
async changes the return type, not how this is bound.

options: [undefined, undefined, undefined]
questions.explanation: All three closures capture the same function-scoped var i, not a copy of its value. By the time they run, the loop has finished and i is 3. With let, each iteration gets a fresh binding and the result would be [0, 1, 2].
rationales: This is the let version, which creates a binding per iteration.
Correct. One shared binding, read after the loop ends.
The variable exists and holds a number when the closures run.
The loop increments i to 3 before the condition fails, so the final value is 3, not 2.

sources.title: let and the TDZ — MDN JavaScript Reference

options: Line 1 logs "undefined" because var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined.
Line 2 logs "b" because function declarations are hoisted with their bodies.
Line 3 logs "c" because the function expression is hoisted with var.
Line 4 logs undefined because let is hoisted like var.
questions.explanation: var hoists the name with the value undefined, and function declarations hoist the whole function, so lines 1 and 2 work. For var c = function..., only the variable is hoisted, so calling it throws TypeError: c is not a function. A let binding is in the temporal dead zone until its declaration, so reading d early throws a ReferenceError.
rationales: Correct. var is hoisted and initialised to undefined.
Correct. Function declarations are fully hoisted.
Only var c is hoisted; c is undefined, so calling it throws a TypeError.
let is in the TDZ; reading it before the declaration throws ReferenceError.

questions.stem: What is the cause and the right fix?
options: The arrow function takes this from the module scope, where it is undefined; use method shorthand label() { ... }.
Template literals cannot access this; use string concatenation.
Object literals in ES modules are frozen; use a class instead.
this.name is shadowed by the module name; rename the property.
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not have their own this; they use the this of the enclosing scope. At the top level of an ES module, this is undefined. Method shorthand gets this from the call site, so service.label() receives service.
rationales: Correct. A lexical this at module top level is undefined; a method binds at call time.
Template literals can read this like any other expression; the problem is which this.
Object literals are not frozen in modules.
There is no shadowing; this is simply undefined here.

options: The arrow function is hoisted to the object, so it sees name.
map binds this to the array for regular functions, and arrays have no name.
Regular functions cannot be passed to map in strict mode.
The regular function is called by map as a plain function, so in strict code its this is undefined; the arrow inherits this from arr(), which was called as o.arr().
questions.explanation: A regular function's this is set by how it is called. map calls the callback without a receiver unless you pass thisArg, so this is undefined in strict code. The arrow function has no this of its own and uses the this of arr(), which is o.
rationales: Arrow functions are not hoisted to objects; they capture lexical this.
Without a thisArg, map does not bind this to the array.
Regular functions are valid map callbacks.
Correct. The call site decides this for regular functions, and arrows use the enclosing this.

questions.scenario: An invoicing service stores line-item prices as JavaScript numbers in dollars (`19.99`) and sums them. Reconciliation finds totals like `59.97000000000001` and equality checks against expected totals fail.
questions.stem: Which approach removes the root cause?
options: Store and sum amounts as integer minor units (cents), converting to a decimal string only for display.
Compare totals with == instead of ===.
Call toFixed(2) after every addition and keep the strings.
Switch every amount to BigInt dollars.
questions.explanation: JavaScript numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so most decimal fractions are approximations and sums accumulate error. Integers up to 2^53 - 1 are exact, so representing money as integer cents keeps arithmetic exact. BigInt dollars cannot represent cents at all.
rationales: Correct. Integer arithmetic within the safe range is exact.
== does no rounding; 59.97000000000001 is still not equal to 59.97.
toFixed returns strings and repeated rounding still drifts, and the next addition would concatenate.
BigInt holds integers only, so dollars as BigInt lose the cents.

questions.scenario: A partner API returns order IDs as JSON numbers, for example `{"id": 9007199254740993}`. After `JSON.parse`, lookups by ID occasionally hit the wrong order.
questions.stem: What is happening and what is the best fix?
options: The ID is parsed as a BigInt, which does not compare equal with ===; convert with Number().
JSON.parse truncates numbers to 32 bits; use parseInt on the raw text.
The ID exceeds Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so it is rounded to a nearby double; ask for IDs as strings (and use BigInt if arithmetic is needed).
Floating-point rounding only affects fractions, so the bug must be elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Doubles represent integers exactly only up to 2^53 - 1 (9007199254740991). 9007199254740993 parses as 9007199254740992, so distinct IDs can collide. Sending the ID as a string preserves every digit, and BigInt can hold it exactly if you need arithmetic.
rationales: JSON.parse never produces BigInt values.
JSON.parse produces doubles, not 32-bit integers; parseInt on the text would also give a double.
Correct. The value is past the safe integer range.
Large integers above 2^53 also lose precision, so rounding explains the collisions.

questions.scenario: A team switches a nanosecond timestamp field from number to bigint in TypeScript.
questions.stem: Which runtime behaviours must the code now handle? (Select two.)
options: Mixing it with numbers, as in ts + 1, throws a TypeError; convert explicitly.
JSON.stringify on an object containing it throws a TypeError unless you convert or supply a replacer.
Division rounds to the nearest integer, so 7n / 2n is 4n.
typeof returns "number" for it, so existing typeof checks keep working.
questions.explanation: BigInt values cannot be mixed with numbers in arithmetic; the operation throws a TypeError, so conversions must be explicit. JSON.stringify does not know how to serialise a BigInt and throws. BigInt division truncates toward zero (7n / 2n is 3n), and typeof gives "bigint".
rationales: Correct. Mixed BigInt and number arithmetic throws.
Correct. JSON has no BigInt support by default.
BigInt division truncates, so the result is 3n.
typeof a BigInt is "bigint", so checks for "number" no longer match.

questions.scenario: A validation helper receives values from `JSON.parse` typed as `any` and must reject `NaN`. It currently uses `if (value === NaN) throw ...`, which never fires.
questions.stem: Which check is correct?
options: isNaN(value), the global function
value == NaN
Number.isNaN(value)
[value].indexOf(NaN) !== -1
questions.explanation: NaN is the only value that is not equal to itself, so both === NaN and == NaN are always false. Number.isNaN returns true only for the actual NaN value. The global isNaN coerces its argument first, so isNaN("abc") is true, and indexOf uses strict equality and cannot find NaN.
rationales: The global isNaN coerces, so strings like "abc" also count as NaN.
Loose equality with NaN is also always false.
Correct. It tests for the NaN value without coercion.
indexOf uses strict equality, so it never finds NaN (includes would).

sources.title: Equality comparisons and sameness — MDN JavaScript Guide

questions.scenario: A leaderboard sorts scores with `scores.sort()`. With `[10, 9, 1]` the result is `[1, 10, 9]`.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: scores.sort((a, b) => a > b)
scores.sort().reverse()
scores.map(Number).sort()
scores.sort((a, b) => a - b)
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, Array.prototype.sort converts elements to strings and compares them in UTF-16 code unit order, so "10" comes before "9". A numeric comparator that returns a negative, zero or positive number sorts numerically.
rationales: A comparator must return a number; a boolean is not a reliable ordering.
Reversing a string-order sort is still string order.
The values are already numbers; the default sort still compares their string forms.
Correct. A numeric comparator sorts by value.

questions.scenario: A code review rule says "always use ===". One function needs to treat both `null` and `undefined` as "missing" but keep `0`, `""` and `false` as real values.
questions.stem: Which condition expresses that most directly?
options: value === undefined
value === null
!value
value == null
questions.explanation: Under loose equality, null and undefined are equal to each other and to nothing else. So value == null is true for exactly those two values and false for 0, "" and false. !value also treats those falsy values as missing, and each strict check covers only one of the two.
rationales: This misses null.
This misses undefined.
This also treats 0, "", false and NaN as missing.
Correct. This is the one widely accepted use of ==.

questions.stem: What do they print?
options: ESM consumer: 0. CommonJS consumer: 1.
Both print 1.
Both print 0.
ESM consumer: 1. CommonJS consumer: 0.
questions.explanation: ES module imports are live bindings to the exporting module's variable, so the importer sees the updated value. In the CommonJS version, module.exports.count was copied from the local variable when the object was created, and destructuring copies it again. Incrementing the local variable does not change either copy.
rationales: This reverses the two module systems' behaviour.
The CommonJS consumer holds a copy taken before inc() ran.
The ESM binding reflects the exporter's updated variable.
Correct. ESM bindings are live and CommonJS values are copied.

questions.scenario: A CommonJS service calls `require("@acme/config")`, a package that recently became ESM-only. On Node 24 the call fails with `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`. Other ESM-only packages load fine through `require`.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: CommonJS cannot load any ES module; rewrite the service as ESM.
require(esm) is disabled in Node 24; upgrade to Node 26.
The package lacks a "require" condition in exports; add one to its package.json locally.
The package's module graph uses top-level await, which require(esm) cannot load synchronously; load it with await import("@acme/config").
questions.explanation: Node can require() an ES module synchronously only if its graph contains no top-level await. If it does, Node throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. Dynamic import() works from CommonJS and handles asynchronous evaluation, and the other packages prove require(esm) itself is available.
rationales: CommonJS can load ES modules through require(esm) without TLA, or through import().
require(esm) works on Node 24; the other packages load.
Patching a dependency's exports does not remove its top-level await.
Correct. Top-level await is the documented reason for this error.

sources.title: Modules: CommonJS modules — Node.js API docs

questions.scenario: A project sets `"type": "module"` in package.json. A script copied from an older codebase, `scripts/seed.ts`, fails at startup on Node 24 with "__dirname is not defined".
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Install @types/node so __dirname is declared.
Add "use strict" at the top of the file.
Rename the file to seed.mjs.
Use import.meta.dirname (or derive it from import.meta.url), because ES modules do not have __dirname.
questions.explanation: With "type": "module", .ts and .js files in that package run as ES modules. ES modules have no __dirname, __filename or require. Node provides import.meta.dirname, import.meta.filename and import.meta.url instead. Adding types only affects the compiler, not the runtime.
rationales: Type declarations do not create runtime globals.
Strict mode does not add CommonJS variables.
.mjs is still ESM, so the error stays. Renaming to .cts would make it CommonJS, but that changes more than the one line.
Correct. This is the ESM equivalent of __dirname.
