questions.scenario: A web server imports a large PDF-rendering library at the top of `server.mjs`, which slows cold starts, although only the `/export` route uses it.
questions.stem: Which statements about switching to dynamic import() are correct? (Select two.)
options: await import("pdf-lib") inside the /export handler defers loading until the route is first used.
import() returns a promise for the module namespace object, so named exports are properties of the awaited result.
import() loads the module synchronously, so the handler does not need to await.
import() is only available in CommonJS files.
questions.explanation: Dynamic import() loads a module at runtime and returns a promise that resolves to the module namespace object. Calling it inside the handler moves the loading cost from startup to the first request that needs it. Module caching means later calls reuse the loaded module. It is available in both ES modules and CommonJS.
rationales: Correct. Loading is deferred to first use.
Correct. You await the namespace and read exports from it.
import() is asynchronous and returns a promise.
import() works in ES modules and CommonJS alike.

questions.stem: What does Node 24 print?
options: a1 start, b1, main, a1 end
a1 start, a1 end, b1, main
main, a1 start, b1, a1 end
a1 start, b1, a1 end, main
questions.explanation: Imports are evaluated before the importing module's body. a1 starts and suspends at its top-level await. b1 does not depend on a1, so it can evaluate meanwhile. main depends on both, so its body waits until a1 finishes. Top-level await delays importers, not unrelated siblings.
rationales: main cannot run until every module it imports, including a1, has finished evaluating.
b1 does not wait for a1's top-level await, since it does not import a1.
Imports are hoisted, so main's body runs last.
Correct. This is the order observed on Node 24.

questions.scenario: An order is typed as `{ isPaid: boolean; isShipped: boolean; trackingNumber?: string }`. Production has orders with `isShipped: true` and no tracking number, and some shipped orders that were never paid.
questions.stem: Which change best prevents these states at compile time?
options: Change `trackingNumber?: string` to `trackingNumber: string | null` so the field is always present.
Keep the type and add JSDoc comments explaining which flag combinations are allowed.
Replace the type with a discriminated union on `status` (draft, paid, shipped) in which only the `shipped` variant has a required `trackingNumber` and only paid and shipped have `paidAt`.
Add a `status` enum alongside the existing booleans and optional field.
questions.explanation: A discriminated union gives each legal state its own shape, so a shipped order without a tracking number cannot be written. Narrowing on `status` then gives access only to fields valid in that state. Making the field nullable or adding a parallel enum still allows contradictory combinations.
rationales: `null` is still allowed when shipped, and the two booleans can still contradict each other.
Comments are not checked by the compiler, so the invalid states remain representable.
Correct. Each variant carries exactly the data valid in that state, so the forbidden combinations cannot be constructed.
A status field next to the old booleans adds a third source of truth that can disagree with the other two.

questions.scenario: `function refund(user: UserId, order: OrderId)` was called with the arguments swapped, and the code compiled. Both IDs are declared as `type UserId = string` and `type OrderId = string`.
questions.stem: What is the most effective way to make the swapped call a compile error?
options: Declare `interface UserId extends String {}` and `interface OrderId extends String {}`.
Brand the types, e.g. `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" }`, and create values only through validating constructors.
Rename the aliases to more distinctive names such as `UserIdentifier` and `OrderIdentifier`.
Change the parameters to an options object `{ user: string; order: string }`.
questions.explanation: TypeScript compares types by structure, not by name, so two string aliases are interchangeable. A brand adds a phantom property that differs between the two types, which makes them mutually unassignable while each stays usable as a string.
rationales: Interfaces are also structural, so two empty extensions of `String` are compatible with each other, and they describe the wrapper object rather than the primitive.
Correct. The differing brand properties make `UserId` and `OrderId` incompatible.
Names do not matter in a structural type system. Both aliases are still `string`.
Named properties help readability, but both are still plain strings and can be filled with the wrong ID.

questions.scenario: After introducing `type Email = string & { readonly __brand: "Email" }`, developers write `input as Email` wherever the compiler complains. Invalid addresses still reach the mailer.
questions.stem: What should the team change?
options: Add a runtime `__brand` property to each email string before sending it.
Replace the brand with a plain `string` alias, since brands evidently do not work.
Allow the `as Email` cast in exactly one function, or use a Zod schema with `.brand<"Email">()`, that validates the value first, and forbid casts elsewhere.
Wrap every send in `try/catch` so that invalid addresses are logged.
questions.explanation: A brand only guarantees what its constructor checks. If any call site can cast, the brand guarantees nothing. Funnelling creation through one validating smart constructor, or a Zod-branded schema whose parse output is branded, makes the brand mean "validated".
rationales: Primitive strings cannot hold properties, and the brand is a compile-time device anyway.
That removes the compile-time distinction instead of fixing how branded values are created.
Correct. With one validating constructor, every `Email` value has passed the check.
This only reports bad data after the fact. The type would still accept unvalidated strings.

questions.scenario: A cache returns JSON that is deserialised into objects typed `{ id: UserId }`, where `UserId` is a branded string. A reviewer suggests guarding with `if (obj.id.__brand !== "UserId") throw ...`.
questions.stem: What is wrong with the suggestion?
options: Nothing. The guard correctly detects unbranded strings.
The brand exists only in the type system. At runtime `__brand` is always undefined, so the guard rejects every value. The data should be re-validated and branded with the smart constructor or schema.
It should use `"__brand" in obj.id` instead of comparing the value.
`JSON.parse` preserves brands, so the guard is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Branding intersects the type with a phantom property that is never set at runtime and is erased on compile. Data from JSON is plain strings, so it must go through the same validation that grants the brand.
rationales: The property is never present, so the guard would throw for valid IDs too.
Correct. Brands are erased, so you validate the format and brand the value again.
The `in` operator throws a TypeError on a primitive string, and the key would not be there anyway.
JSON carries only data. Type information, including brands, is never serialised.

questions.scenario: With `strict` enabled, `catch (e) { logger.error(e.message) }` fails with TS18046.
questions.stem: Which fix is type-safe and handles every value that might be thrown?
options: Annotate the variable: `catch (e: Error)`.
Cast it: `logger.error((e as Error).message)`.
Narrow it: `logger.error(e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e))`.
Set `useUnknownInCatchVariables: false` in tsconfig.
questions.explanation: Under strict, catch variables are `unknown` because JavaScript can throw any value. Narrowing with `instanceof Error` handles Error objects and falls back safely for strings and other values. A catch annotation may only be `any` or `unknown`.
rationales: Catch clause annotations other than `any` or `unknown` are a compile error.
The cast compiles but is a lie when a string or plain object is thrown: `.message` is undefined.
Correct. It narrows `unknown` safely and covers non-Error throws.
This switches back to `any` and hides the problem everywhere instead of handling it.

questions.stem: Which two statements about typing errors in TypeScript are accurate? (Select two.)
options: A function's type does not record which exceptions it may throw.
The `reason` parameter of a `promise.catch(...)` callback is typed `any`, and `useUnknownInCatchVariables` does not change that.
A catch variable can be annotated with any subclass of `Error`, such as `catch (e: HttpError)`.
`strict` mode leaves `useUnknownInCatchVariables` off; it has to be enabled separately.
questions.explanation: TypeScript has no checked exceptions or `throws` clause, so thrown types are invisible to callers. `useUnknownInCatchVariables` is part of `strict` but only applies to `try/catch` bindings. Promise rejection callbacks declare `reason: any` in the standard library typings, so they stay `any`.
rationales: Correct. Signatures list parameters and return types only.
Correct. Rejection reasons in `.catch` and `.then` callbacks are `any`, so narrow them explicitly.
Only `any` or `unknown` are allowed as catch clause annotations.
`useUnknownInCatchVariables` is one of the flags that `strict` turns on.

questions.scenario: `loadConfig(path)` can fail because the file is missing, the JSON is malformed or a field is invalid. Callers must handle each case differently, and today they often forget to.
questions.stem: Which return type makes the failure modes visible and forces callers to handle them?
options: `Config | undefined`, returning undefined on any failure.
`Config`, throwing a `ConfigError` subclass for each case.
`[Error | null, Config | null]`, Go style.
`{ ok: true; value: Config } | { ok: false; error: { kind: "missing" | "syntax" | "invalid"; detail: string } }`
questions.explanation: A discriminated Result union puts the failure kinds in the signature, and `value` cannot be read without narrowing on `ok`. `undefined` loses the reason, thrown errors do not appear in the type, and a tuple of two nullable slots does not link the error slot to the value slot.
rationales: This discards which failure happened, so callers cannot respond differently.
Thrown types do not appear in the signature, so nothing forces callers to catch them.
Narrowing one slot does not narrow the other, so `Config | null` remains after checking the error.
Correct. Failures are values in the type, and narrowing on `ok` is required.

questions.scenario: After adopting Result types, a team proposes wrapping every function, including ones that can only fail through programmer bugs such as an impossible `switch` default, so that nothing ever throws.
questions.stem: Which guideline is the most sensible?
options: Return Results for every function without exception, so the codebase never uses `throw`.
Return Results for expected, recoverable failures that callers should handle. Let bugs and violated invariants throw, and catch them at a top-level boundary that logs and responds.
Return to exceptions everywhere, because Result types are not a TypeScript language feature.
Return `null` for recoverable failures and throw for everything else.
questions.explanation: Result types are a design pattern for making expected failures explicit. Bugs and broken invariants have no meaningful local recovery, so they belong at a central `try/catch` boundary. Forcing every call site to unwrap impossible errors adds noise without adding safety.
rationales: This pushes impossible cases into every signature and buries the real failure modes in noise.
Correct. Expected failures become values, and defects throw to a boundary handler.
Being a pattern rather than a feature does not make it less useful for expected failures.
`null` loses the failure reason that callers need.

questions.scenario: A handler does `const body = (await req.json()) as CreateUser;` where `CreateUser` is a hand-written interface. Malformed bodies cause 500s deep in the service layer.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Call `Schema.parse(body)` and let any `ZodError` propagate to the generic 500 handler.
Keep the cast and add a Zod schema maintained alongside the interface.
Define a Zod schema, call `safeParse` on the body, return 400 on failure, use `result.data`, and derive `CreateUser` with `z.infer<typeof Schema>`.
Change the cast to `as unknown as CreateUser` to make the intent explicit.
questions.explanation: A cast does no runtime checking. Parsing with a schema validates the body and returns a typed, cleaned value. Deriving the type with `z.infer` keeps the runtime check and the static type from drifting, and `safeParse` makes it easy to answer with 400 instead of 500.
rationales: This validates, but it reports a client mistake as a server error.
Two hand-maintained definitions drift apart over time.
Correct. You get one source of truth, a runtime check at the boundary, and a proper client error.
A double cast is still unchecked and only hides the problem more thoroughly.

questions.scenario: A signup schema is `z.object({ name: z.string() })`. A client sends `{ "name": "Ana", "isAdmin": true }`. Security wants such requests rejected rather than silently accepted.
questions.stem: In Zod 4, what happens today, and what should you use instead?
options: The parse fails today. No change is needed.
`isAdmin` is stripped from the output today. Use `z.strictObject({ name: z.string() })` to reject unknown keys.
`isAdmin` is passed through today. Use `z.object(...).strip()`.
`isAdmin` is stripped today. Use `z.looseObject(...)` to reject it.
questions.explanation: By default `z.object` strips unrecognised keys from the parsed output. In Zod 4, `z.strictObject` makes unknown keys a validation failure, and `z.looseObject` keeps them. These replace the older `.strict()` and `.passthrough()` methods.
rationales: `z.object` does not fail on extra keys. It removes them.
Correct. Strict objects reject unknown keys.
The default strips the key rather than passing it through, and stripping is not rejection.
`z.looseObject` keeps unknown keys, which is the opposite of what is wanted.

questions.scenario: The server schema is `z.object({ email: z.email(), role: z.enum(["user","admin"]).default("user") })`. The web form's type is `z.infer<typeof Schema>`, and the form fails to compile because it does not set `role`.
questions.stem: Which type should the form use?
options: `z.input<typeof Schema>`, in which `role` is optional because the default is applied during parsing.
`Partial<z.infer<typeof Schema>>`.
`z.infer<typeof Schema>` with `role` filled in manually as `"user"`.
`typeof Schema`.
questions.explanation: `z.infer` is the output type after parsing, where defaults have been applied, so `role` is required there. `z.input` describes what the schema accepts, where a defaulted field is optional. Callers that send data should use the input type.
rationales: Correct. The input type models what callers send before defaults apply.
This makes `email` optional too, which is wrong for the form.
This duplicates the server default on the client, and the two can drift.
That is the schema object's own type, not the type of the data.

questions.scenario: A developer writes `const r = Schema.safeParse(input); if (r.success) save(input);`
questions.stem: Why is this a mistake?
options: `safeParse` throws on failure, so the `if` is redundant.
`safeParse` does not narrow `input`. The validated and cleaned value, with unknown keys removed and defaults or transforms applied, is `r.data`, and that is what should be saved.
`r.success` is always true unless `parse` was called first.
`input` is narrowed, but `save` needs `z.input`.
questions.explanation: Parsing returns a new value. It does not turn the original variable into a typed one. Downstream code should use `r.data`, which carries the inferred type and is the version with extra keys stripped and defaults applied.
rationales: `safeParse` never throws. It returns a success or error object.
Correct. Use the parsed output, not the raw input.
`safeParse` works on its own. `success` reflects the result.
`safeParse` is not a type guard on its argument, so `input` keeps whatever type it had before the call.

questions.stem: You are upgrading a codebase from Zod 3 to Zod 4. Which three changes match the Zod 4 migration guide? (Select three.)
options: Replace `{ message: "..." }` with `{ error: "..." }` when customising errors.
Replace `z.string().email()` with the top-level `z.email()`.
Give every `z.record(...)` both a key schema and a value schema.
Replace `z.enum([...])` with `z.nativeEnum(...)`.
questions.explanation: Zod 4 deprecates `message` in favour of `error`, moves string formats to top-level functions such as `z.email()`, and requires two arguments for `z.record`. It deprecates `z.nativeEnum` in favour of `z.enum`, which is the reverse of the last option.
rationales: Correct. `message` is deprecated in favour of `error`.
Correct. Method-form string formats are deprecated.
Correct. The single-argument form of `z.record` is gone.
This is backwards. `z.nativeEnum` is deprecated and `z.enum` is preferred.

questions.scenario: The server and client share `type Order = { id: string; createdAt: Date }`. The client does `const o = (await res.json()) as Order; o.createdAt.getTime();` and crashes with "getTime is not a function", even though everything type-checks.
questions.stem: What is the root cause, and what is the best fix?
options: The client has an old cached bundle. Bust the cache.
The server should send `createdAt.getTime()` as a number while the shared type stays `Date`.
Add `"lib": ["dom"]` so the client knows about `Date`.

JSON serialises the Date as an ISO string, and the cast hides that. Share a schema of the wire format and parse responses on the client, for example with `z.coerce.date()`, or type the field as `string` and convert it explicitly.
questions.explanation: A shared TypeScript type describes in-memory values, but `JSON.stringify` turns a Date into a string, so the client actually receives a string. The `as` cast tells the compiler otherwise. Parsing the response with a shared schema keeps the static type and the runtime value consistent.
rationales: Caching is unrelated. The value is a string on every request.
This changes the runtime value but keeps the type lying about it.
`Date` types are already available, and the problem is the runtime value, not the declarations.
Correct. Types stop at the wire, so parse or model the serialised shape.

questions.scenario: The web client imports `Order` from the server's `orders.ts` module, which also imports the database driver. The client bundle has grown by the size of the driver.
questions.stem: Which change keeps the shared type and removes the server code from the client?
options: Copy the `Order` interface into the client by hand.
Import with `import * as Server from "..."` and reference `Server.Order`.
Use `import type { Order } from "..."`, ideally from a small shared contracts package, so the import is erased at compile time.
Mark the server module with `"sideEffects": false` and rely on tree shaking.
questions.explanation: A type-only import is removed entirely from the emitted JavaScript, so the server module is never loaded by the client. Under `verbatimModuleSyntax`, importing a type without `type` is an error (TS1484), which catches this mistake early. A contracts package keeps the dependency graph clean.
rationales: Copying removes the dependency but creates two definitions that drift.
A namespace import is still a value import, so the module is still loaded.
Correct. Type-only imports leave nothing behind at runtime.
Tree shaking is best effort, and it does not make a runtime import of server code safe.

questions.scenario: A TypeScript service validates every request with Zod schemas. It is opening its API to partner teams who write Go and Python, and they want a contract they can generate clients from.
questions.stem: Which approach keeps a single source of truth?
options: Send partners the exported TypeScript types from the contracts package.
Generate JSON Schema or OpenAPI from the existing Zod schemas (Zod has built-in JSON Schema conversion) and publish the generated spec from CI.
Write an OpenAPI document by hand and keep the Zod schemas as they are.
Document the endpoints in a README with example payloads.
questions.explanation: TypeScript types are erased and mean nothing to Go or Python toolchains, so partners need a language-neutral contract. Generating that contract from the schemas the server already enforces keeps the specification and the runtime validation identical. A hand-written spec next to the schemas will drift.
rationales: Other languages cannot consume TypeScript types.
Correct. The published spec is derived from the schemas that actually run.
Two hand-maintained descriptions of the same API will diverge.
Prose and examples cannot be used to generate typed clients.

questions.scenario: Importing the untyped JavaScript package `legacy-lib` fails under `strict` with TS7016, "Could not find a declaration file for module 'legacy-lib'". No `@types/legacy-lib` exists. The app uses two of its functions.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Add `// @ts-ignore` above the import.
Turn off `noImplicitAny` in the project.
Add `declare module "legacy-lib";` so the import resolves.
Add a `.d.ts` file with `declare module "legacy-lib" { ... }` that declares the two functions with accurate signatures.
questions.explanation: When no community types exist, a small hand-written ambient module declaration types exactly what you use and keeps type checking on. The shorthand `declare module "legacy-lib";` resolves the error but makes every import `any`, so it is a last resort.
rationales: This suppresses the error and leaves the module as `any`, and it can hide other errors on that line.
This weakens type checking across the whole project to fix one import.
This works, but every export becomes `any`. Use it only as a last resort.
Correct. The declaration is minimal, accurate and keeps type safety.

questions.scenario: To add a `user` field to a framework's `Request` interface, a developer creates `types/augment.d.ts` that contains only `declare module "some-framework" { interface Request { user?: User } }`. After that, imports such as `import { createServer } from "some-framework"` start failing.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: Augmentation only works in `.ts` files, not in `.d.ts` files.

The file has no top-level `import` or `export`, so it is a script. Its `declare module` block declares a new ambient module that shadows the package's real types instead of augmenting them. Adding `export {}` or `import "some-framework"` fixes it.
Interfaces cannot be merged across packages.
`user` must be declared as required, because augmentations cannot add optional members.
questions.explanation: A `declare module "x"` block is a module augmentation only when it appears inside a module. In a script file it is an ambient module declaration, which can replace the package's real typings. Making the file a module turns the block back into an augmentation that merges with the real declarations.
rationales: Augmentations work in declaration files as long as the file is a module.
Correct. Without a top-level import or export, the block is a declaration, not an augmentation.
Interface merging across module boundaries is exactly what module augmentation does.
Optional members are fine. The problem is how the file is classified.

questions.stem: Which two statements about module augmentation match the TypeScript handbook? (Select two.)
options: An augmentation can only patch existing declarations. It cannot add new top-level declarations to the module.
Default exports cannot be augmented, only named exports.
`declare global { ... }` works only in script files that have no imports or exports.
An augmentation can change the type of an existing interface property, for example from `string` to `number`.
questions.explanation: The handbook notes two limits: you cannot declare new top-level declarations in an augmentation, and you cannot augment default exports. Global augmentation with `declare global` is done from inside a module. Merged property declarations must have identical types.
rationales: Correct. Augmentations patch what already exists.
Correct. Only named exports can be augmented.
`declare global` is how a module adds to the global scope.
Merged properties must have the same type, so this is an error.

questions.scenario: Your team is publishing an internal npm library written in TypeScript, but the package contains only compiled JavaScript. Consumers with strict settings get TS7016 ("Could not find a declaration file for module"), and consumers without noImplicitAny see the imports typed as `any`.
questions.stem: What should the team do?
options: Ask consumers to add `declare module "@acme/lib";` in their projects.
Enable `declaration: true`, ship the generated `.d.ts` files in the package, and point `types` (or the `"types"` condition in `exports`) at them.
Publish the types to DefinitelyTyped as `@types/acme__lib`.
Publish the `.ts` sources and ask consumers to compile them.
questions.explanation: The publishing guide says that a package written in TypeScript should bundle its own declaration files and reference them from package.json. DefinitelyTyped is meant for packages that do not ship their own types. The shorthand ambient module only makes the `any` explicit.
rationales: This confirms the `any` instead of providing types.
Correct. Emit declarations and point package.json at them.
DefinitelyTyped is for packages that do not bundle their own types. Yours can ship them directly.
This pushes a build step onto every consumer and depends on their compiler settings.

questions.scenario: A service has strict: true. A bug report shows a crash reading .name of undefined in code like const first = users[0]; log(first.name). The compiler never complained.
questions.stem: Which tsconfig change would have made the compiler flag this line?
options: Enable strictNullChecks
Enable exactOptionalPropertyTypes
Enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess
Set target to esnext
questions.explanation: noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds | undefined to array element and index-signature reads, so users[0] becomes User | undefined and first.name is an error. It is not part of strict, so it stays off even though strict is on. strictNullChecks is already enabled by strict.
rationales: Already on under strict; it does not add undefined to index reads.
Concerns optional properties, not array indexing.
Correct: it types users[0] as possibly undefined.
target affects emitted syntax and default lib, not index checks.

questions.scenario: An API patch type is { nickname?: string }. The server treats a missing key as "leave unchanged" and an explicit undefined (sent as null after a mapping layer) as "clear it". Developers keep accidentally writing { nickname: undefined }.
questions.stem: Which setting makes the type system distinguish "missing" from "present but undefined" here?
options: useUnknownInCatchVariables
noUncheckedIndexedAccess
strictPropertyInitialization
exactOptionalPropertyTypes
questions.explanation: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes, nickname?: string means the key may be absent but may not hold undefined, so { nickname: undefined } errors (TS2375). Code that really wants to clear the value must then use a type that says so explicitly. The other flags address unrelated checks.
rationales: Types catch variables as unknown.
Adds undefined to index reads; it does not restrict optional properties.
Checks class fields are initialized in the constructor.
Correct: it separates absent from undefined for optional properties.

questions.scenario: A team targets Node 24 in production but set "target": "esnext" so that every new API would type-check. A release crashes because Map.prototype.getOrInsert is undefined, although tsc reported no errors.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Set target/lib to the ES level the deployed runtime supports, so APIs it lacks are type errors
Keep esnext and add "DOM" to lib
Switch moduleResolution to bundler
Enable skipLibCheck
questions.explanation: target and lib only describe which syntax and APIs the compiler assumes; they never add polyfills. With esnext, newer APIs type-check even though Node 24 does not provide them. Matching lib to the real runtime turns those calls back into compile errors.
rationales: Correct: the declared lib should reflect what the runtime actually provides.
DOM declarations do not provide Map methods and are wrong for a server.
Module resolution has no effect on built-in API declarations.
Skipping .d.ts checks hides errors rather than revealing missing APIs.

questions.scenario: After upgrading a Node project from TypeScript 5.x to 7.0 with an unchanged tsconfig (no "types" entry), every reference to process and Buffer now reports "Cannot find name". @types/node is still installed.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: strict now defaults to true; set strict: false
The types default is now [], so add "types": ["node"]
@types/node is incompatible with TS 7; uninstall it
Add "DOM" to lib
questions.explanation: Since TypeScript 6.0 the types option defaults to an empty list, so installed @types packages are no longer loaded automatically. Adding "types": ["node"] restores the Node globals. Turning off strict or adding DOM does not supply Node declarations.
rationales: strict does not control which global declarations load.
Correct: the new default no longer includes @types packages automatically.
The package is fine; it is simply not included.
DOM does not declare process or Buffer.

questions.scenario: A repo holds two apps: an API server compiled by tsc and run with node dist/server.js, and a React front end built by Vite. One shared base tsconfig currently uses moduleResolution bundler for both.
questions.stem: Which configuration best matches how each app resolves modules?
options: Server: module nodenext; front end: moduleResolution bundler
Both: moduleResolution bundler
Both: module nodenext
Server: moduleResolution node10; front end: bundler
questions.explanation: The modules guide says to model the system that resolves imports at runtime: Node for the server and the bundler for the front end. Using bundler for the server lets extensionless imports compile that Node will reject. node10 resolution was removed in TypeScript 7.0.
rationales: Correct: each app is checked against its real resolver.
Hides Node-only errors such as missing extensions in the server.
Forces needless extension rules on bundled code; bundler fits Vite.
node10 no longer exists in 7.0 and never modelled exports correctly.

questions.scenario: A package has "type": "module" and module nodenext. src/index.ts contains import { sum } from "./math"; and tsc reports that relative imports need an explicit file extension.
questions.stem: Which change fixes the error while keeping tsc emit?
options: Add baseUrl: "."
Switch to moduleResolution node10
Write import { sum } from "./math.js"
Rename index.ts to index.tsx
questions.explanation: In Node ESM, relative specifiers must be complete, and TypeScript under nodenext enforces this. You write the extension of the emitted file (.js), and TypeScript maps it to math.ts while checking. An alternative is writing ./math.ts with rewriteRelativeImportExtensions.
rationales: baseUrl is removed in 7.0 and does not affect extension rules.
Removed in 7.0, and it would only hide the runtime failure.
Correct: the specifier matches what Node will load at runtime.
The file extension of the importer is irrelevant.

questions.scenario: A team runs services with node src/main.ts (Node type stripping). Startup fails with "The requested module ./types.ts does not provide an export named Config". types.ts exports only an interface Config, and main.ts has import { Config } from "./types.ts".
questions.stem: Which tsconfig option would have caught this at compile time?
options: verbatimModuleSyntax
skipLibCheck
noUncheckedSideEffectImports
declaration
questions.explanation: Node strips only the annotations and keeps the import as written, so it asks the module for a runtime export that does not exist. Under verbatimModuleSyntax, importing a type without the type modifier reports TS1484. The fix is import type { Config } (or an inline type modifier).
rationales: Correct: it requires import type for type-only names, which Node then drops.
Only skips checking declaration files.
Concerns imports with no bindings such as CSS files.
Controls .d.ts emit, not import elision.

questions.scenario: A developer wants to run an existing codebase directly with Node type stripping (no transform flags).
questions.stem: Which constructs will Node reject as unsupported TypeScript syntax? (Select two.)
options: enum Color { Red, Green }
constructor(private readonly db: Db) {} (parameter properties)
interface Config { port: number }
const cfg = { port: 3000 } satisfies Config
questions.explanation: Node can only erase syntax that has no runtime meaning. Enums and parameter properties generate JavaScript, so Node throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. Interfaces and satisfies are purely type-level and erase cleanly.
rationales: Correct: enums produce a runtime object.
Correct: parameter properties produce field assignments.
Interfaces erase completely.
satisfies is erased along with the type.

questions.scenario: Developers keep adding enums to a codebase that runs under Node type stripping, and each one is discovered only when the service fails to start.
questions.stem: What is the most effective way to surface these problems in the editor and CI?
options: Set target to es2015
Enable isolatedDeclarations
Run Node with --experimental-transform-types
Enable erasableSyntaxOnly in tsconfig
questions.explanation: erasableSyntaxOnly reports TS1294 for enums, parameter properties and other non-erasable syntax, matching what Node stripping accepts. --experimental-transform-types was removed in Node 26, so it is not a durable answer. The other options do not address runtime syntax.
rationales: Downlevelling syntax does not ban enums.
Requires explicit export types; unrelated to enums.
Removed in Node 26; it only postpones the problem.
Correct: it mirrors Node stripping limits at compile time.

questions.scenario: A team bumped typescript to 7.0 in package.json. tsc builds are much faster, but typescript-eslint and the Vue template type checker now fail to start.
questions.stem: What is the recommended way to keep both working?
options: Wait for those tools to drop TypeScript integration
Downgrade the whole repo to TS 5.x
Point typescript-eslint at the tsc 7 binary with a custom path
Keep TS 7 for tsc and give API-based tools TS 6 via @typescript/typescript6 (for example an npm alias)
questions.explanation: TypeScript 7.0 has no programmatic API; it is planned for 7.1. The 7.0 announcement recommends installing @typescript/typescript6 for tools that need the API, often by aliasing it. That keeps the fast native compiler for builds.
rationales: Not a plan; the bridge exists today.
Gives up the speedup without need.
A binary path does not provide the JS API these tools import.
Correct: this is the documented bridge for API consumers.

questions.scenario: On TypeScript 7.0, a build fails with TS5102 "Option 'baseUrl' has been removed". The config has baseUrl: "./src" and paths: { "@app/*": ["app/*"] }.
questions.stem: What is the correct migration?
options: Move the options into a separate jsconfig.json
Add ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"
Pin --stableTypeOrdering false
Remove baseUrl and rewrite paths relative to the tsconfig, e.g. "@app/*": ["./src/app/*"]
questions.explanation: baseUrl is removed in 7.0, and paths entries resolve relative to the tsconfig without it. ignoreDeprecations was a 6.0-only bridge; 7.0 still accepts the flag, but the removed options stay removed.
rationales: Same compiler, same error.
Does not restore removed options in 7.0.
Unrelated to module paths.
Correct: paths without baseUrl is the replacement.

questions.scenario: An engineering manager asks what to expect from moving a large monorepo type-check from TypeScript 6 to 7.0.
questions.stem: Which statement is best supported by the TypeScript 7.0 announcement?
options: Speed is unchanged; only memory use drops
Builds become exactly 10x faster on every codebase
Full builds are typically several times faster (about 8x to 12x on the published projects), partly from parallel type checking
Gains only appear when every project is converted to isolatedDeclarations
questions.explanation: The announcement reports roughly 8x to 12x faster builds on projects such as vscode and sentry, plus lower memory, using --checkers parallelism by default. It does not promise a fixed multiplier for every codebase, so you should measure your own.
rationales: Both speed and memory improve.
Overstates a headline as a guarantee.
Correct: matches the published range and mechanism.
No such prerequisite exists.

questions.scenario: A monorepo with 30 packages links them using tsconfig paths only. Every app type-check re-checks the source of all shared packages, and CI time keeps climbing.
questions.stem: Which change gives packages real build boundaries?
options: Add more paths aliases so resolution is faster
Merge all packages into one tsconfig with include: ["packages/**"]
Turn off strict in shared packages
Give shared packages composite: true, add references from consumers and build with tsc --build
questions.explanation: With project references, each composite project builds once and emits declarations. Consumers then check against those .d.ts files instead of re-checking source, and tsc --build skips projects that are up to date. paths only redirects resolution, so it provides no boundary.
rationales: Aliases do not stop the source from being checked.
Makes one huge program, the opposite of a boundary.
Reduces safety and barely affects time.
Correct: this is what project references are for.

questions.scenario: CI for a project-references monorepo runs tsc -b from a clean checkout on every push and takes too long.
questions.stem: Which two changes most directly speed up repeated builds? (Select two.)
options: Persist .tsbuildinfo files (incremental output) between CI runs
Enable skipLibCheck so dependency .d.ts files are not re-checked
Pass --singleThreaded to TypeScript 7
Replace references with paths aliases
questions.explanation: Incremental builds use .tsbuildinfo to re-check only what changed, which helps only if that file survives between runs. skipLibCheck avoids checking declaration files from dependencies, often a large share of build time. --singleThreaded turns off TS 7 parallelism, and paths removes the build graph.
rationales: Correct: lets tsc -b skip unchanged work.
Correct: removes a common large cost.
Slower: it disables parallel checking.
Loses up-to-date checks and boundaries.

questions.scenario: A "type": "module" library emits JavaScript to dist/ and declarations to a separate types/ folder, and ships "exports": { ".": { "import": "./dist/index.js", "types": "./types/index.d.ts" } }. Consumers on moduleResolution nodenext get implicit-any errors as if no declarations exist.
questions.stem: What is the problem?
options: "types" is only read by bundler resolution
TypeScript ignores exports; add a top-level "typings" field instead
The path must use .d.mts
Conditions match in key order and the first match wins, so "import" matches before "types"; put "types" first
questions.explanation: Node and TypeScript evaluate exports conditions in object key order, and the first match wins. Here "import" matches first and resolves to ./dist/index.js, so "types" is never reached. TypeScript tries extension substitution on that path, but there is no ./dist/index.d.ts because the declarations live in types/, so the import is untyped. Node docs say the "types" condition should always come first.
rationales: nodenext reads it too.
TypeScript honours exports under nodenext/bundler, and top-level fields do not override it.
A .d.ts file is fine for an ESM package with "type": "module"; the extension is not the problem.
Correct: order matters and types must lead.

questions.scenario: A dual package emits dist/index.js (ESM) and dist/index.cjs (CJS), but both "import" and "require" conditions point "types" at a single dist/index.d.ts in a "type": "module" package. CJS consumers see a wrong default-import shape.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Delete the "require" condition and rely on main
Emit a declaration per format (e.g. index.d.cts for the CJS build) and nest "types" under each condition
Add esModuleInterop: false for consumers
Put "default" first so either format is found
questions.explanation: A declaration file has a module format, inferred from its extension and package type just as for JavaScript. A single .d.ts in a module package claims to be ESM, which misdescribes the CJS build. Separate declarations for each format, each under its own condition, describe each entry accurately.
rationales: Exports takes precedence; main does not fix the types.
Correct: each entry gets declarations that match its format.
Setting it false is removed in 7.0, and it is a consumer setting anyway.
default must be last, or it shadows other conditions.

questions.scenario: A platform team wants a fast tool to generate .d.ts files for each file in parallel, without running the full type checker.
questions.stem: Which setting makes that possible and what does it require from authors?
options: emitDeclarationOnly; no JavaScript may be emitted
isolatedModules; every import must include a file extension
composite; every file must be in include
isolatedDeclarations; exported functions and values need explicit type annotations
questions.explanation: isolatedDeclarations ensures each file's declaration output can be produced from that file alone. It requires explicit types where inference would otherwise be needed; an unannotated return such as return a + 1 reports TS9013.
rationales: Skips JS emit but still type-checks to produce declarations.
isolatedModules concerns JS emit, not declarations, and does not require extensions.
Enables references but still relies on the checker for .d.ts.
Correct: this is its purpose and its cost.

questions.scenario: After moving to TypeScript 7, a React app built by Vite reports an error on import "./global.css" saying the module cannot be resolved. The import works fine at runtime.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Set moduleResolution to classic
Remove the import and load the CSS from index.html only
Add an ambient declaration such as declare module "*.css" {}
Add // @ts-ignore above every CSS import
questions.explanation: noUncheckedSideEffectImports is on by default since TypeScript 6.0, so side-effect imports must resolve to something TypeScript knows about. A wildcard ambient module tells the checker that CSS imports are valid. This keeps typo detection for real module imports.
rationales: classic resolution is removed in 7.0.
Changes the app to satisfy the checker unnecessarily.
Correct: declares the asset module pattern once.
Suppresses errors line by line and hides real typos.

questions.scenario: A team switches a CLI from tsc emit to node src/cli.ts. Source files use import { db } from "@lib/db" via tsconfig paths, and relative imports like "./util" without extensions.
questions.stem: Which two changes are needed for Node type stripping to load the code? (Select two.)
options: Replace the @lib alias with a package.json "imports" entry such as "#lib/*"
Add explicit extensions to relative imports, e.g. "./util.ts"
Add baseUrl so Node can find @lib
Enable sourceMap so stripped files map back to source
questions.explanation: Node does not read tsconfig, so paths aliases do not resolve. The package.json "imports" field with # specifiers is the Node-native replacement. Node also requires full file extensions in specifiers. Source maps are unnecessary because types are replaced with whitespace.
rationales: Correct: Node resolves # imports itself.
Correct: Node requires explicit extensions.
Node ignores tsconfig, and baseUrl is removed in TS 7.0.
Not needed: stripping preserves positions.

questions.scenario: A library is transpiled by esbuild file by file. barrel.ts contains export { User } from "./user"; where User is an interface, and the esbuild output fails at runtime looking for a User export.
questions.stem: Which option makes tsc flag this pattern before esbuild ever sees it?
options: incremental
noImplicitAny
declarationMap
isolatedModules (or the stricter verbatimModuleSyntax)
questions.explanation: A single-file transpiler cannot know that User is only a type, so it keeps the re-export. isolatedModules reports such re-exports and requires export type, and verbatimModuleSyntax enforces the same rule more broadly. The other options do not model single-file transpilation.
rationales: Only caches build state.
Concerns missing type annotations.
Only affects .d.ts source maps.
Correct: these flags exist for single-file transpilers.

questions.scenario: A TypeScript service on Node 24 calls a pricing API. Under load the upstream sometimes hangs for minutes, and sometimes answers 503. The current code is `const res = await Promise.race([fetch(url), sleep(2000).then(() => { throw new Error('timeout') })]); return res.json();` inside a try/catch.
questions.stem: Which change fixes both the leaked hung requests and the unnoticed 503 responses?
options: Keep the race but raise the timeout to 30 seconds so fewer requests are abandoned.
Call `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) })` and throw when `res.ok` is false.
Wrap `res.json()` in its own try/catch, because a 503 body will fail to parse.
Replace `fetch` with `http.get`, because global `fetch` cannot be cancelled in Node.
questions.explanation: A raced timer settles the outer promise but never cancels the request, so hung sockets pile up. Passing an AbortSignal aborts the request itself. `fetch` resolves on HTTP error statuses, so the code must check `res.ok` to notice a 503.
rationales: A longer timeout still leaves the request running after the race settles, and it does nothing about 503s.
Correct. The signal really aborts the request, and the `ok` check catches 4xx/5xx responses that fetch resolves normally.
A 503 can carry a valid JSON body; relying on a parse failure is not a status check.
Node's global fetch supports cancellation through `AbortController` and `AbortSignal`.

questions.scenario: A log-archiving job does `createReadStream(src).pipe(createGzip()).pipe(createWriteStream(dst))`. When a source file is deleted mid-run, the process slowly runs out of file descriptors and the job never reports a failure.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Add `.on('error', console.error)` to the read stream only.
Use `await pipeline(src, gzip, dst)` from `node:stream/promises` and handle the rejection.
Increase the process file descriptor limit.
Read the whole file with `readFile` first, then gzip it in memory.
questions.explanation: `.pipe()` does not forward errors or destroy the other streams when one fails, so handles leak and nothing reports the failure. `pipeline` destroys every stream on error and returns a promise that rejects, which the job can await and report.
rationales: Logging the error does not close the gzip and write streams, so the leak remains.
Correct. pipeline propagates errors, cleans up all streams and gives an awaitable result.
That hides the leak for longer without fixing it.
It avoids streams but loads large logs fully into memory and does not address error handling design.

questions.scenario: An API server computes a password-hardening hash in pure JavaScript for each signup. While it runs, p99 latency for every other route spikes. The team wants to keep a single Node process.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the latency spikes?
options: Mark the hashing function `async` and `await` it.
Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` so the hash runs on libuv's thread pool.
Run the hashing in a pool of `Worker` threads from `node:worker_threads` and post results back.
Schedule the hash with `process.nextTick` so requests are served first.
questions.explanation: CPU-bound JavaScript blocks the event loop no matter how it is wrapped. The Node docs describe worker threads as useful for CPU-intensive JavaScript, so moving the hash to a worker pool frees the main thread to serve other requests.
rationales: An async function still runs its synchronous code on the main thread.
libuv's pool serves certain built-in async operations; it never runs your JavaScript.
Correct. Workers run JavaScript on separate threads, which is their intended use.
nextTick callbacks run before the event loop continues, so this blocks just as much.

questions.scenario: A containerised Node HTTP service is stopped by its orchestrator with SIGTERM and force-killed 30 seconds later. Deploys currently drop in-flight requests and leave transactions open.
questions.stem: Which two changes make shutdown graceful? (Select two.)
options: In a `SIGTERM` handler, call `server.close()`, await the in-flight requests, then close the database pool.
Register a `SIGKILL` listener that flushes pending writes before the process dies.
Start an unref'd deadline timer in the handler that calls `process.exit(1)` if cleanup has not finished in time.
Move the database cleanup into a `process.on('exit')` listener that awaits `pool.end()`.
questions.explanation: `server.close()` stops new connections while in-flight work completes, and the handler can then close resources. A deadline timer guarantees the process exits before the orchestrator's force kill even if cleanup hangs. SIGKILL cannot be listened for, and 'exit' listeners must be synchronous.
rationales: Correct. Stop intake, finish in-flight work, then release resources.
SIGKILL cannot have a listener; the process is terminated immediately.
Correct. A hard deadline prevents a hung cleanup from blocking exit until the force kill.
'exit' listeners must be synchronous, so the awaited `pool.end()` never completes.

questions.scenario: A job queue extends `EventEmitter` and calls `this.emit('error', err)` when a job fails. Nobody registered an `'error'` listener. A single failing job takes down the whole process. Elsewhere, startup code waits for readiness with `await once(queue, 'ready')`.
questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains the crash and the behaviour of the startup code?
options: Emitting `'error'` throws only in CommonJS; in ESM it is converted to a warning.
Emitting `'error'` with no listener is silently ignored; the crash must come from an unhandled rejection elsewhere.
Emitting `'error'` only throws when the emitter is typed with an event map; `once()` ignores errors.
Emitting `'error'` with no listener makes Node throw the error; `once()` rejects if `'error'` is emitted while it waits.
questions.explanation: The events documentation states that an `'error'` event with no listener is thrown, which usually crashes the process, so emitters need an `'error'` listener. `events.once` returns a promise that rejects if `'error'` is emitted while waiting, so the startup code sees the failure.
rationales: The module format does not change EventEmitter error semantics.
The 'error' event is special: without a listener it is thrown, not ignored.
TypeScript typings have no runtime effect, and once() does reject on 'error'.
Correct. This matches the documented behaviour of 'error' events and events.once.

questions.scenario: A handler for `POST /orders` starts with `const body: CreateOrder = await req.json();` where `CreateOrder` is a hand-written interface. A client sent `quantity: "5"` as a string and corrupted totals downstream. The project's `lib` includes `DOM`, and type-checking passes.
questions.stem: Which two changes give the handler real input safety? (Select two.)
options: Define a Zod schema and call `schema.safeParse(await req.json())`, returning 400 with `z.flattenError` details on failure.
Replace the annotation with `(await req.json()) as CreateOrder` so the intent is explicit.
Derive the type with `type CreateOrder = z.infer<typeof schema>` instead of maintaining a separate interface.
Enable `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` so the compiler rejects string quantities.
questions.explanation: With the DOM lib, `req.json()` is typed `any`, so the annotation is an unchecked claim. Runtime validation with `safeParse` rejects bad input, and deriving the static type from the schema keeps type and validator from drifting. Neither assertions nor compiler flags inspect runtime data.
rationales: Correct. Validation at the boundary is the only thing that checks the actual bytes.
`as` is still a compile-time assertion with no runtime check.
Correct. A single source of truth means the type always matches what was validated.
Compiler flags cannot see the request body at runtime.

questions.scenario: Auth middleware sets the current user. The team declared `user?: User` on a globally augmented request type, so every handler now writes `req.user!.id`, and one public route accidentally reads `req.user!` and throws at runtime.
questions.stem: Which design best expresses "this handler always has a user" in the type system?
options: Change the augmentation to `user: User` (non-optional) so the `!` assertions can be removed.
Keep the augmentation and add a lint rule banning non-null assertions.
Store the user in a module-level variable set by the middleware.
Wrap protected handlers in a higher-order `withUser(next)` that authenticates and calls `next(req, { ...ctx, user })` with a context type that includes `user: User`.
questions.explanation: A global augmentation applies to every handler, so it can only be optional (honest) or required (a lie on public routes). A wrapper that passes typed context gives protected handlers a non-optional user and gives unprotected handlers no user at all. The type now follows the actual control flow.
rationales: This makes public routes claim a user they never get, so the runtime bug becomes invisible to the compiler.
Banning `!` forces null checks everywhere but still does not tie the user to protected routes.
Module-level state is shared across concurrent requests and is unsafe.
Correct. The wrapper's type parameter makes the user present exactly where authentication ran.

questions.scenario: A handler loads `const row = await db.users.find(id)` (type `UserRow`, which includes `passwordHash`), then does `const dto: UserDto = row; return Response.json(dto);`. `UserDto` has only `id` and `email`. A security review finds hashes in API responses.
questions.stem: Why did this compile, and what is the right fix?
options: Structural typing lets a type with extra properties be assigned to `UserDto`, and types are erased; build the DTO explicitly or parse it with a `z.object` output schema that strips unknown keys.
`Response.json` ignores TypeScript types; switching to `new Response(JSON.stringify(dto))` fixes it.
The excess property check is disabled by `skipLibCheck`; turning it off would have caught the leak.
`UserDto` should be declared as a `class` so that assignment copies only its fields.
questions.explanation: Assignability is structural: extra properties are allowed except on fresh object literals, so `row` is a valid `UserDto`. Types have no runtime effect, so the hash is still on the object when serialised. Building the response object or parsing through a stripping schema removes it.
rationales: Correct. The leak comes from structural assignability plus type erasure, and only a runtime mapping removes the field.
Both serialise every own property of the object; the hash leaks either way.
skipLibCheck only skips declaration files; excess property checks never apply to a variable.
Assigning to a class-typed variable does not copy or filter fields at runtime.

questions.scenario: A public webhook endpoint must reject payloads that contain any key not in its schema, so that misspelled fields are reported to the sender instead of being dropped. The schema is currently `z.object({ event: z.string(), id: z.uuid() })` in Zod 4.
questions.stem: What should the team change?
options: Call `.passthrough()` on the schema.
Keep `z.object`; it already rejects unknown keys by default.
Use `z.strictObject({ ... })`, which fails parsing when unknown keys are present.
Use `z.looseObject({ ... })` and compare key counts manually.
questions.explanation: In Zod 4, `z.object` strips unknown keys, `z.strictObject` rejects them, and `z.looseObject` keeps them. Rejecting unknown keys is exactly what `z.strictObject` does, and `.passthrough()` is the deprecated form of loose behaviour.
rationales: passthrough keeps unknown keys (and is deprecated in favour of z.looseObject); it does not reject them.
z.object silently strips unknown keys rather than rejecting them.
Correct. strictObject turns unknown keys into a validation error.
looseObject keeps unknown keys; manual counting re-implements what strictObject provides.

questions.scenario: After upgrading to React 19 types, `const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>();` fails with TS2554 "Expected 1 arguments, but got 0".
questions.stem: What is the recommended type-safe replacement for this DOM ref, and what is the type of `inputRef.current`?
options: `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)`; `current` is `HTMLInputElement | null`.
`useRef<HTMLInputElement | undefined>()`; `current` is `HTMLInputElement | undefined`.
`useRef<HTMLInputElement>(undefined!)`; `current` is `HTMLInputElement`.
`createRef<HTMLInputElement>()`; `current` is `HTMLInputElement`.
questions.explanation: React 19 made the `useRef` argument required. Passing `null` for a DOM ref gives a `RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null>`, so code must handle the null case before React attaches the element. All refs are now mutable, so no separate mutable variant is needed.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented React 19 pattern for DOM refs.
Omitting the argument is exactly what React 19's types reject.
The non-null assertion lies: current really is undefined until the element mounts.
createRef makes a new ref on every render in a function component and is not the hook replacement.

questions.scenario: A design-system team is rewriting `TextInput` for React 19. Consumers must be able to pass any native input attribute (`placeholder`, `onBlur`, `aria-*`) and a ref to focus the input.
questions.stem: Which two choices fit React 19 and TypeScript best? (Select two.)
options: Type props as `ComponentProps<"input"> & { label: string }` and spread the rest onto `<input>`.
Wrap the component in `forwardRef`, because function components cannot receive `ref` otherwise.
Accept `ref` as a regular prop and pass it to the inner `<input ref={ref}>`.
Declare each supported native attribute by hand so the public API stays explicit.
questions.explanation: `ComponentProps<"input">` inherits every native input attribute and its event types. In React 19, `ref` is a regular prop for function components, so the component can forward it without `forwardRef`.
rationales: Correct. Inheriting native props keeps the wrapper complete and correctly typed.
React 19 passes ref as a prop to function components; forwardRef is no longer needed for new code.
Correct. Destructure ref and attach it to the inner element.
Hand-written attributes drift from the DOM and miss aria-* and event props.

questions.scenario: A `Select` component is typed as `{ options: unknown[]; getLabel: (o: unknown) => string; onChange: (o: unknown) => void }`. Every caller casts inside `onChange`, and a recent bug came from casting to the wrong type.
questions.stem: What is the best way to type this component?
options: Change `unknown` to `any` so callers no longer need casts.
Make it a generic function component `function Select<T>(props: { options: T[]; getLabel: (o: T) => string; onChange: (o: T) => void })` so `T` is inferred from `options`.
Type it as `React.FC<SelectProps>` and add an overload per option type.
Keep `unknown` and add a runtime `typeof` check inside `Select`.
questions.explanation: A generic component lets TypeScript infer `T` from the `options` prop at each call site, so `getLabel` and `onChange` receive the caller's real item type with no casts. Generic components are written as generic functions, which a `React.FC` annotation cannot express directly.
rationales: any removes the casts by removing the checking, so the same bug would compile silently.
Correct. Inference ties all three props to the same item type.
React.FC cannot carry a free type parameter, and overloads per type do not scale.
Select cannot know the caller's domain type, so runtime typeof checks cannot recover it.

questions.scenario: A `Layout` component declares `children: JSX.Element`. Under React 19 types, the build reports that the global `JSX` namespace is not found, and teammates also complain that `<Layout>Loading…</Layout>` was always rejected.
questions.stem: Which children type fixes both problems?
options: `children: React.ReactElement`
`children: React.JSX.Element`
`children: string | JSX.Element`
`children: React.ReactNode`
questions.explanation: `React.ReactNode` accepts JSX elements, strings, numbers, null and arrays, which is what children can be. `ReactElement` and `JSX.Element` accept only JSX elements, and in React 19 the global `JSX` namespace has moved to `React.JSX`.
rationales: ReactElement accepts only JSX elements, so the string child is still rejected.
This fixes the namespace but still rejects the string child.
The global JSX namespace is gone in React 19, and this still misses numbers, null and arrays.
Correct. ReactNode is the documented type for anything renderable as children.

questions.scenario: After the React 19 types upgrade, `<div ref={(el) => (nodeRef = el)} />` now fails to compile, although it worked before.
questions.stem: Why, and what is the fix?
options: Ref callbacks were removed in React 19; use `useRef` instead.
Ref callbacks may now return a cleanup function, so an implicit non-function return is rejected; use a block body `ref={(el) => { nodeRef = el; }}`.
`el` is now typed `unknown`; annotate it as `(el: HTMLDivElement) => ...`.
Callback refs must be memoised with `useCallback` to type-check.
questions.explanation: React 19 lets ref callbacks return a cleanup function, so its types reject callbacks that implicitly return anything else. An arrow with an assignment expression body returns the element, so it must become a block body.
rationales: Ref callbacks still exist and gained cleanup support in React 19.
Correct. The block body returns undefined, which the new type accepts.
el is typed as the element or null; the problem is the return value.
Memoisation affects identity, not whether the return type checks.

questions.scenario: A test does `vi.mock("./db")` and then `getUser.mockResolvedValue({ id: "u1" })`, where `getUser` is imported from `./db`. The test runs, but type-checking reports that `mockResolvedValue` does not exist on the function type.
questions.stem: What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Cast with `(getUser as any).mockResolvedValue(...)`.
Move the `vi.mock` call below the import so TypeScript sees the mock.
Use `vi.mocked(getUser).mockResolvedValue({ id: "u1" })`.
Disable type checking for test files in tsconfig.
questions.explanation: `vi.mock` replaces the module at runtime, but the import keeps its original static type. `vi.mocked` is a type helper that returns the same object typed as a mock, so the mock API and the resolved value are both type-checked.
rationales: any silences the error and also stops checking the mocked value against the real return type.
vi.mock is hoisted to the top of the file regardless, and placement does not change the import's type.
Correct. vi.mocked adds mock typing while preserving the function's signature.
This throws away type safety in all tests to work around one helper call.

questions.scenario: A library adds `expectTypeOf(parseConfig(raw)).toEqualTypeOf<Config>()` to `config.test.ts`. A refactor changes the return type to `Partial<Config>`, CI runs `vitest run`, and the test still passes.
questions.stem: Why did the test pass, and what should the team do?
options: `expectTypeOf` is a no-op at runtime; move type assertions to a `*.test-d.ts` file and run `vitest --typecheck` in CI.
`Partial<Config>` is identical to `Config` for type tests; add a runtime assertion instead.
`toEqualTypeOf` only checks assignability; switch to `toExtend` for exact matching.
Vitest caches type results; clear the cache before each CI run.
questions.explanation: Type assertions do nothing when the test executes; they only fail when the file is type-checked. Vitest type tests live in `*.test-d.ts` files and run under `vitest --typecheck`, where type errors count as failures.
rationales: Correct. Without a type-check step the wrong assertion can never fail.
Partial<Config> makes every property optional, which is a different type.
It is the reverse: toEqualTypeOf is exact and toExtend is assignability.
Caching is not the cause; the assertions were never type-checked.

questions.scenario: A public helper returns `{ id: string; name: string; createdAt: Date }`. The team wants a type test that keeps passing when new fields are added, but fails if `id` or `name` disappear or change type.
questions.stem: Which assertion fits?
options: `assertType<any>(result)`
`expectTypeOf(result).toEqualTypeOf<{ id: string; name: string }>()`
`expectTypeOf(result).toBeObject()`
`expectTypeOf(result).toExtend<{ id: string; name: string }>()`
questions.explanation: `toExtend` checks that the actual type is assignable to the expected shape, so extra properties are allowed but missing or retyped `id` and `name` fail. `toEqualTypeOf` requires an exact match and would fail as soon as a field is added.
rationales: Asserting against any accepts everything.
The exact match already fails today because of createdAt.
Any object passes, so removing id or name would not be caught.
Correct. Assignability is exactly "at least this shape".

questions.scenario: In an order handler, `audit.record(order)` (which returns a promise) is called without `await`. When the audit store is down, rejections are lost and records silently disappear. Reviews missed it twice.
questions.stem: Which typescript-eslint rule is designed to catch this?
options: `no-explicit-any`
`switch-exhaustiveness-check`
`no-unsafe-assignment`
`no-floating-promises`
questions.explanation: `no-floating-promises` reports promises that are not awaited, returned, or handled with a rejection handler, unless explicitly discarded with `void`. That is exactly the forgotten `await` here, and the rule uses type information to know the call returns a promise.
rationales: This flags explicit any annotations, not unhandled promises.
This checks that a switch covers every union member.
This flags any values assigned to variables, not unhandled promises.
Correct. It targets unhandled promise-valued statements.

questions.scenario: A permission check was made async: `async function canEdit(u: User, doc: Doc): Promise<boolean>`. One call site still reads `if (canEdit(user, doc)) { save(doc); }`, and every user can now edit every document. Type-checking passes.
questions.stem: Which typescript-eslint rule reports this call site?
options: `no-floating-promises`, because the promise is never awaited.
`await-thenable`, because `canEdit` returns a thenable.
`no-misused-promises`, because a promise is used in a conditional where it is always truthy.
`no-unnecessary-type-assertion`, because the condition is asserted to be boolean.
questions.explanation: A promise object is always truthy, so the condition always passes. `no-misused-promises` checks for promises in conditionals (and async functions passed where a void return is expected). `no-floating-promises` targets promise-valued statements that are dropped, not promises used as conditions.
rationales: The promise is consumed by the if, so it is not a floating statement.
await-thenable flags awaiting a non-thenable, the opposite situation.
Correct. Its conditional check exists for exactly this always-truthy bug.
There is no type assertion in the code.

questions.scenario: A monorepo has moved to TypeScript 7.0 for type-checking. The team adds `no-floating-promises` to its flat ESLint config, and linting fails because the rule requires type information.
questions.stem: Which two steps are needed for typed linting to work? (Select two.)
options: Use a `*TypeChecked` config such as `recommendedTypeChecked` with `parserOptions.projectService: true`.
Set `"strict": true` in tsconfig, which turns on type information for ESLint.
Make typescript-eslint resolve TypeScript 6 through the `@typescript/typescript6` npm alias, because TS 7.0 has no programmatic API.
Switch the rule to a `// eslint-disable` comment at the top of each file until TS 7.1.
questions.explanation: Typed rules need the parser to build type information, which `projectService` provides alongside the type-checked configs. typescript-eslint depends on the TypeScript compiler API, which TS 7.0 does not ship, so the 7.0 release post recommends running such tools on TS 6 via the `@typescript/typescript6` alias.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented typed-linting setup.
Compiler strictness does not give ESLint type information.
Correct. Tools that need the compiler API run on TS 6 under 7.0.
Disabling the rule removes the protection the team wanted.

questions.scenario: A 400k-line codebase never set `strict` in tsconfig. After upgrading to TypeScript 7.0, type-checking reports thousands of new errors, mostly implicit `any` and possible `null`. The release must ship this sprint.
questions.stem: Which migration strategy is most appropriate?
options: Run a codemod that inserts `// @ts-ignore` above every error line and keep `strict` on.
Enable `skipLibCheck`, which suppresses errors in application code during migration.
Stay on TypeScript 5.x indefinitely, since strict mode cannot be turned off in 7.0.
Set `"strict": false` explicitly to keep the old behaviour, then enable strict sub-flags one at a time, using `@ts-expect-error` for deferred fixes.
questions.explanation: TS 6.0 and 7.0 default `strict` to true, so the errors come from a changed default, not new bugs. Pinning `strict: false` isolates the upgrade; enabling `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks` and the rest one at a time keeps each step reviewable. `@ts-expect-error` fails once a suppressed error is fixed, so suppressions do not go stale.
rationales: Blanket @ts-ignore hides errors permanently, including ones introduced later on those lines.
skipLibCheck skips declaration files only; application errors remain.
strict can still be set to false in 7.0; only some legacy options were removed.
Correct. Separate the version upgrade from the strictness migration and tighten incrementally.

questions.scenario: A service parses webhook bodies with `const payload = JSON.parse(text);` and passes `payload.amount` into billing code. A malformed webhook sent `amount: "12.50"` and billing concatenated strings. The project already uses type-checked linting.
questions.stem: Which typescript-eslint rule family flags the root cause at the parse site and downstream uses?
options: `no-floating-promises`, because `JSON.parse` may be asynchronous.
`no-unsafe-*` rules such as `no-unsafe-assignment` and `no-unsafe-member-access`, which flag `any` values flowing into typed code.
`switch-exhaustiveness-check`, because `amount` has an unhandled case.
`no-misused-promises`, because the value is used in arithmetic.
questions.explanation: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, which disables checking for everything derived from it. The `no-unsafe-*` rules report assigning, accessing members of, calling, passing or returning `any`, which pushes the code to validate the payload into a real type first.
rationales: JSON.parse is synchronous and returns no promise.
Correct. These rules exist to stop any from leaking into typed code.
There is no switch statement over a union here.
No promise is involved.

questions.scenario: A reducer handles `type Action = { type: "add" } | { type: "remove" } | { type: "clear" }` with a `switch` that has no `default`. A teammate adds `{ type: "undo" }` to the union, and the new action is silently ignored at runtime.
questions.stem: Which lint rule reports the missing case as soon as the union changes?
options: `no-floating-promises`
`no-unsafe-assignment`
`switch-exhaustiveness-check`
`no-misused-promises`
questions.explanation: `switch-exhaustiveness-check` uses type information to report a `switch` over a union that does not handle every member. It complements the compile-time `never` check in a `default` branch and catches switches that lack one.
rationales: This targets unhandled promises.
This targets any values being assigned.
Correct. It reports unhandled union members in switch statements.
This targets promises used in conditionals or void-return positions.
